entry.title: Profiling Task Lifetimes and Main-Actor Contention in Swift

link.title: Profiling Task Lifetimes and Main-Actor Contention in Swift

entry.content:
Concurrency problems that survive code review and testing usually show up as time: a screen that takes 300 ms longer to appear than it should, a scroll that hitches, a request that never finishes, a battery that drains because hundreds of tasks were alive when a dozen would do. Thread-based profiling tools struggle with all of them, because in Swift concurrency the interesting thing is not what a thread is doing, but what each task is doing, including the many tasks that are not on any thread at all.

Instruments’ Swift Concurrency template records exactly that: every task’s state over time, what each one is waiting for, how long actors’ queues get, and where custom intervals begin and end. This article records real traces of a deliberately unhealthy program, reads the measurements that matter, and connects each pattern to its fix, from both Instruments and the command line.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled with the Swift 6.4 toolchain and traced with xctrace from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. Numbers quoted below come from those traces. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift.

What the template records

The Swift Concurrency template combines several instruments:

  • Swift Tasks records each task’s creation, state changes, and end, along with its name, priority, the actor it is running on, and the task or continuation it is waiting for.
  • Swift Actors records each actor’s queue of pending jobs over time.
  • A time profiler samples call stacks, attributed to tasks as well as threads.
  • Points of Interest shows intervals and events emitted with OSSignposter.

The task states are the vocabulary for everything that follows. As they appear in the trace:

State Meaning
Creating Created, and has not yet started running
Enqueued Ready to run, waiting for its executor or actor to pick it up
Running Executing on a thread
Suspended Paused at an await, not occupying a thread
Waiting Suspended specifically waiting for another task, such as a child or a task’s value
Continuation Suspended in withCheckedContinuation or similar, waiting for resume 
stateDiagram-v2
    accTitle: Task states recorded by the Swift Tasks instrument
    [*] --> Creating
    Creating --> Running: executor picks it up
    Running --> Suspended: await that suspends
    Running --> Waiting: awaits another task
    Running --> Continuation: withCheckedContinuation
    Suspended --> Enqueued: awaited work completes
    Waiting --> Enqueued: awaited task finishes
    Continuation --> Enqueued: resume called
    Enqueued --> Running: executor or actor becomes free
    Running --> [*]: returns or throws

A healthy task spends its life mostly Running or Suspended on useful waits. Long stretches in Creating or Enqueued mean the task wanted to run and could not. A task that ends a trace in Continuation, and stayed there, is the signature of a leaked continuation.

Recording a trace

In Xcode, choose Product, then Profile, then the Swift Concurrency template, and record while exercising the feature under investigation. The same recording works from the command line, which makes it scriptable:

xcrun xctrace record --template 'Swift Concurrency' --output run.trace --launch -- ./workload
xcrun xctrace export --input run.trace --toc
xcrun xctrace export --input run.trace \
    --xpath '/trace-toc/run[@number="1"]/data/table[@schema="SwiftTaskStateTable"]'

The --toc export lists every table the trace contains; the Swift Concurrency ones include SwiftTaskStateTable, SwiftActorQueueSize, SwiftTotalTaskCountAll, and SwiftParallelRunningTasks. Each table exports as XML, one row per state interval, with repeated values compressed into id and ref attributes. A short script that resolves the references and sums durations per task and state turns a trace into numbers a CI job can compare between builds.

The program under the microscope

The workload contains four patterns worth finding, each in a named task. Names, set with Task(name:) and addTask(name:) in Swift 6.2 (SE-0469), are what make a trace with hundreds of tasks readable:

import Foundation

actor Store {
    private(set) var count = 0

    func add() {
        count += 1
    }
}

@MainActor
final class Model {
    var value = 0
}

func busyWork(milliseconds: Int) {
    let clock = ContinuousClock()
    let deadline = clock.now + .milliseconds(milliseconds)
    while clock.now < deadline {}
}

/// Pattern 1: a long synchronous job on the main actor.
@MainActor
func blockMainActor() {
    busyWork(milliseconds: 300)
}

@concurrent
func renderThumbnail(_ index: Int) async -> Int {
    busyWork(milliseconds: 5)
    return index
}

let model = Model()
let store = Store()

/// Pattern 2: a named fan-out of 40 children, created while the main actor is about to be busy.
let fanOut = Task(name: "thumbnail-fanout") {
    await withTaskGroup(of: Int.self) { group in
        for index in 0..<40 {
            group.addTask(name: "thumbnail-\(index)") { await renderThumbnail(index) }
        }
        var total = 0
        for await value in group { total += value }
        return total
    }
}

/// Pattern 3: thousands of fine-grained hops between the main actor and another actor.
let chatty = Task(name: "chatty-store-calls") {
    for _ in 0..<3_000 {
        await store.add()
        model.value += 1
    }
}

blockMainActor()
_ = await fanOut.value
await chatty.value

/// Pattern 4: a task whose continuation is never resumed.
let stuck = Task(name: "stuck-request") {
    await withCheckedContinuation { (_: CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>) in }
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
let storedCount = await store.count
assert(model.value == 3_000 && storedCount == 3_000)

Running it prints a continuation misuse warning for the stuck task at exit, as the checked continuations article describes. In a large app, that warning may never be seen; the trace shows the same problem visually.

Reading the trace

Summing the task-state table per task gave, for the run with a 300 ms main-actor block:

Task Creating Enqueued Running Notable
thumbnail-fanout 300.3 ms   9.7 ms Its 40 children each ran about 5 ms
chatty-store-calls 308.7 ms 91.1 ms 215.5 ms 3,000 round trips to Store
stuck-request 0.1 ms   0.05 ms 310.5 ms in Continuation, until the process exited

With the main-actor block shortened to 120 ms in a second run, the Creating times of the first two tasks dropped to 120.3 and 131.9 ms. Each pattern points to a specific fix.

Pattern 1: tasks that cannot start

thumbnail-fanout and chatty-store-calls spent 300 ms in Creating: created, ready, and unable to run. Both were created in top-level code, which is main-actor isolated, so both were main-actor tasks. Task { } inherits the main actor’s isolation, as the task lifetime article shows, and the main actor was busy with a 300 ms synchronous job. The Creating time tracked the length of the block exactly: 300 ms in one run, 120 ms in the other.

This is how main-actor contention looks in a trace: tasks waiting in Creating or Enqueued while the main thread’s lane shows one long Running interval. In an app, the same 300 ms is a frozen UI: about 18 dropped frames at 60 Hz, using the frame-budget formula from the main actor article. The fix is to find the long main-actor job in the time profiler, usually by selecting the main thread during the stall, and move its computation to a @concurrent function.

Pattern 2: fan-out that behaves

The 40 children of thumbnail-fanout each ran for about 5 ms and spent a millisecond or so suspended or waiting to start. The Swift Actors instrument showed the global concurrent executor’s queue peaking at 16 pending jobs while the 40 children were scheduled onto the 20-thread pool. That is a healthy shape: work queued briefly and drained at the rate the hardware allowed. A task group that adds thousands of children at once would show the queue size climbing much higher, and the total task count rising with it; that is the cue to use the sliding window from the task groups article.

Pattern 3: chatty actor calls

chatty-store-calls made 3,000 round trips: main actor to Store, then back. It accumulated 91 ms Enqueued, waiting for the main actor or the store to pick it up after each hop, and 215 ms Running. Two observations follow.

First, the Enqueued time is pure scheduling overhead, spread across 6,000 executor switches. The actors article measured those switches at about 6 µs per round trip without tracing. Batching the work into one call to Store, with one hop back to apply the result, removes almost all of it.

Second, the Running time is inflated by the instrument itself: about 72 µs per iteration under tracing, an order of magnitude more than the same loop takes untraced. The Swift Tasks instrument records every state change, and this loop changes state constantly. Compare traces with traces, before and after a change under the same instrument, not traced timings with untraced ones.

Pattern 4: a task that never finishes

stuck-request entered the Continuation state almost immediately and stayed there for the rest of the run. In the timeline, it is a lane that never ends. Selecting it shows its creation backtrace, which leads to the withCheckedContinuation call that never had a matching resume. The task’s name is what makes this findable among hundreds of short-lived tasks.

The same lane appears for the deadlocks in the deadlocks article that involve no blocked thread: a task suspended in Waiting on another task that is itself suspended. The task-state table’s “Waiting For” column records which task each one is waiting on, which turns a silent hang into a chain you can follow.

Utilization, not just duration

A trace window also gives utilization directly. If the main thread is Running for \(T_{\text{busy}}\) out of a window \(T\), its utilization is

\[\rho = \frac{T_{\text{busy}}}{T}.\]

The waiting-time formula from the actors article, \(W_q = \frac{\rho}{1 - \rho}\,s\) for jobs of mean length \(s\), explains why a main actor that is busy “only” 70% of the time during a scroll still feels sluggish: each new job, such as a touch or an animation update, waits on average more than twice the length of a typical job before it starts. The goal for the main actor during interaction is not “under 100% busy” but “mostly idle.”

For scrolling and animation in apps, Apple’s preferred metric is the hitch time ratio: milliseconds of hitches per second of animation. The Animation Hitches instrument and XCTest’s performance metrics report it; Apple’s guidance in Eliminate animation hitches with XCTest treats under 5 ms/s as good, 5 to 10 ms/s as worth investigating, and above 10 ms/s as critical.

Custom intervals with OSSignposter

Task states show how tasks spent their time. Signposts show what they were doing in your app’s terms: “decode feed,” “apply search results,” “prefetch page 3.” An OSSignposter interval appears in the Points of Interest lane, aligned with the task lanes:

import os

let signposter = OSSignposter(subsystem: "com.example.feed", category: .pointsOfInterest)

@concurrent
func decodeFeed(itemCount: Int) async -> Int {
    let interval = signposter.beginInterval("decode feed", id: signposter.makeSignpostID(), "items: \(itemCount)")
    defer { signposter.endInterval("decode feed", interval) }
    busyWork(milliseconds: 20)
    return itemCount
}

for batch in 0..<3 {
    _ = await decodeFeed(itemCount: batch * 10)
}
signposter.emitEvent("feed ready")

Traced with the same template, this produced three “decode feed” intervals of 20.0 ms each, carrying their metadata, “items: 0”, “items: 10”, and “items: 20”, in the OSSignpostIntervals table. Signposts cost very little when no tool is recording, so they can stay in production code. They are the most effective way to connect a trace to a user-visible operation, and the natural boundaries for performance tests that measure an operation’s duration across builds.

Tools for apps on devices

The traces above came from a command-line program on a Mac. On a device, add:

  • Hangs, which flags main-thread unresponsiveness above a threshold. It watches an app’s main run loop, so it reports nothing for a command-line tool; in the recordings above its table stayed empty even with a 300 ms block.
  • Animation Hitches, for frame-level timing during scrolling and transitions.
  • Thread Performance Checker, enabled in a scheme’s Diagnostics, which flags priority inversions and main-thread work that is known to be slow, at run time while debugging.
  • MetricKit hang and CPU diagnostics, which report what real users experienced in the field.
  • A main-actor heartbeat, as in the main actor article, for a cheap continuous measurement during tests.

A workflow

  1. Name tasks that represent user-visible operations or long-lived work. Unnamed tasks appear only as numbers.
  2. Add signposts around operations whose duration matters to users.
  3. Record the scenario, not the whole app: one screen opening, one search, one scroll.
  4. Look for long Creating or Enqueued intervals on tasks that should start promptly. Find the job occupying their executor.
  5. Look for lanes that do not end: tasks in Continuation or Waiting at the end of the scenario.
  6. Check counts and queues: total live tasks and actor queue sizes during the scenario. Steady growth means unbounded fan-out or leaked tasks.
  7. Fix one thing and record again, comparing the same tables before and after.

Summary

  • The Swift Concurrency template records task states, waits, actor queues, and signposts; xctrace records and exports the same data from the command line.
  • Long Creating or Enqueued intervals mean tasks could not run. In the traces above, two tasks waited 300 ms behind a 300 ms main-actor job, and 120 ms behind a 120 ms one.
  • Chatty cross-actor calls show up as Enqueued time spread across thousands of hops; batching removes it.
  • A lane that stays in Continuation is a leaked continuation; Waiting chains reveal async deadlocks.
  • The instrument adds overhead, about 72 µs per hop in the chatty loop, so compare traces with traces.
  • Main-actor utilization \(\rho\) predicts responsiveness through \(\rho / (1 - \rho)\); for animation, track the hitch time ratio.
  • Name tasks and add OSSignposter intervals so traces speak in terms of your app’s operations.

Exercise

Take the search model from the stale results article and drive it with a scripted burst of typing in a test target. Record it with the Swift Concurrency template twice: once with debouncing disabled and once with an 80 ms quiet period. Add a signpost around each search request. From the exported tables, report the number of search tasks created, the number that reached Running, the total time spent in requests that were later superseded, and the main actor’s utilization during the burst, and explain the differences.

Further reading

  • Visualize and optimize Swift concurrency, WWDC22, the introduction to the Swift Concurrency instruments.
  • Analyze hangs with Instruments, WWDC23.
  • Recording performance data with OSSignposter.
  • SE-0469: Task Naming.

entry.title: Finding Data Races in Swift with Thread Sanitizer

link.title: Finding Data Races in Swift with Thread Sanitizer

entry.content:
Swift 6 proves the absence of data races at compile time, for code it can check. Every real codebase also contains code it cannot: classes marked @unchecked Sendable, globals marked nonisolated(unsafe), modules still in Swift 5 mode, @preconcurrency imports, Objective-C and C, and anything built on unsafe pointers. Those escape hatches exist for good reasons, and each one is a place where a data race can still hide.

Thread Sanitizer (TSan) checks the other way around: at run time, for the code paths a test actually executes. It instruments every memory access, tracks which accesses are ordered by synchronization, and reports any two conflicting accesses that are not. This article runs TSan on races that compile cleanly in Swift 6 mode, shows how to read its reports, measures its overhead, and describes how to make it a routine part of testing.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled with the Swift 6.4 toolchain and run on macOS 26 with -sanitize=thread. The reports quoted below are real output from those runs, trimmed for width. Mutex requires iOS 18, macOS 15, or later.

What TSan detects, and how

A data race is two accesses to the same memory location, from different threads, at least one of them a write, with no happens-before ordering between them. Happens-before is the ordering created by synchronization: unlocking a mutex happens before the next lock of it, resuming a continuation happens before the resumed code runs, a task’s creation happens before its first instruction.

TSan tracks happens-before with vector clocks. Each thread \(t\) keeps a vector \(V_t\) with one counter per thread. A thread increments its own entry as it runs; synchronization operations merge vectors, taking the element-wise maximum. An access \(a\) by thread \(t\) happens before an access \(b\) by thread \(u\) exactly when

\[V_a[t] \le V_b[t],\]

that is, when \(u\) had, by the time of \(b\), observed thread \(t\)’s progress up to \(a\) through some chain of synchronization. TSan stores the clock of recent accesses in shadow memory next to each location. When a new access arrives, it compares clocks; if neither access happens before the other and at least one is a write, it reports a race.

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: Unsynchronized writes race, while writes ordered by a lock do not
    participant A as Task A
    participant M as Memory: hits
    participant B as Task B
    Note over A,B: Without synchronization
    A->>M: write hits
    B->>M: write hits, no happens-before edge from A, TSan reports a race
    Note over A,B: With a Mutex
    A->>M: lock, write hits, unlock
    Note over A,B: unlock happens before the next lock
    B->>M: lock, write hits, unlock, ordered after A, no report

Two properties follow from this design:

  • TSan reports races that happen in the run, not races that could happen. If a test never executes the racy path, or never runs it on two threads, TSan says nothing. Coverage and concurrency in tests determine what it can find.
  • TSan does not need the race to cause a wrong result. It reports the unsynchronized pair even when the timing happened to work out. That is why it finds bugs that stress testing alone misses.

Swift’s concurrency runtime is annotated for TSan, so task creation, await, actor hops, and continuations all establish happens-before. Correctly isolated Swift concurrency code produces no reports.

Enabling it

  • Xcode: Edit Scheme, then Run or Test, then Diagnostics, then enable Thread Sanitizer. It applies to the scheme’s builds and test runs.
  • SwiftPM: swift build --sanitize=thread, swift test --sanitize=thread.
  • swiftc: swiftc -sanitize=thread.

TSan runs on macOS and on iOS, tvOS, and watchOS simulators, not on physical devices. It cannot be combined with Address Sanitizer in the same build. Debug builds give the most readable reports; optimized builds find races that only appear at speed. Running both, periodically, is ideal.

On the test machine, outside Xcode, TSan’s default symbolizer stalled when the first report was printed. Setting TSAN_OPTIONS="external_symbolizer_path=" made it fall back to its built-in symbolization, which prints function names without line numbers. Xcode symbolizes reports fully and was not affected.

A race that compiles cleanly

This program compiles in Swift 6 mode without a warning. Both of its races are behind escape hatches that tell the compiler “trust me”:

import Foundation

/// Claims to be Sendable, but nothing protects `storage`.
final class SessionCache: @unchecked Sendable {
    private var storage: [String: Int] = [:]

    func record(_ key: String) {
        storage[key, default: 0] += 1
    }

    var count: Int { storage.count }
}

nonisolated(unsafe) var hits = 0

@concurrent
func hammer(_ cache: SessionCache) async {
    await withTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
        for worker in 0..<4 {
            group.addTask {
                for request in 0..<200 {
                    cache.record("key-\((worker * 200 + request) % 50)")
                    hits += 1
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

let cache = SessionCache()
await hammer(cache)
print("entries:", cache.count, "hits:", hits)

Without TSan, the program usually prints something plausible and occasionally crashes inside Dictionary, because concurrent writes can corrupt its storage. On one run it printed hits: 740: 60 of 800 increments were lost, because hits += 1 is a read and a write, and two threads interleaved them.

Under TSan, the first report was:

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: Swift access race (pid=65781)
  Modifying access of Swift variable at 0x000109803870 by thread T3:
    #0 race.SessionCache.record(Swift.String) -> ()
    #1 (1) suspend resume partial function for closure #1 () async -> () in
       closure #1 (inout Swift.TaskGroup<()>) async -> () in race.hammer(race.SessionCache) async -> ()
    #2 swift::runJobInEstablishedExecutorContext(swift::Job*)

  Previous modifying access of Swift variable at 0x000109803870 by thread T1:
    #0 race.SessionCache.record(Swift.String) -> ()
    #1 (1) suspend resume partial function for closure #1 () async -> () in
       closure #1 (inout Swift.TaskGroup<()>) async -> () in race.hammer(race.SessionCache) async -> ()
    #2 swift::runJobInEstablishedExecutorContext(swift::Job*)

  Location is heap block of size 24 at 0x000109803860 allocated by main thread:
    #0 malloc
    #2 async_Main

  Thread T3 (tid=21157131, running) is a GCD worker thread
  Thread T1 (tid=21157129, running) is a GCD worker thread

SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: Swift access race in race.SessionCache.record(Swift.String) -> ()

In total the run produced seven warnings, for the dictionary and for the hits global, and the process exited with a failure status.

Reading a report

Every TSan report has the same parts, and each answers a specific question:

Part Question it answers
First line: “Swift access race” or “data race” What kind of conflict. A Swift access race means two overlapping Swift accesses, such as two mutations of a stored property; a data race is the underlying memory-level conflict.
First stack Which code made the access that was just detected
“Previous … access” stack Which code made the earlier, conflicting access
“Location is …” What memory it was: a heap block and where it was allocated, or a named global such as 'r2.hits : Swift.Int'
Thread descriptions Which threads were involved. In async code these are usually GCD worker threads of the cooperative pool

For async code, the frames are partial functions: the pieces of an async function between suspension points, as the async/await article describes. “suspend resume partial function for closure #1 … in hammer” means “the body of the first child task in hammer, after a suspension point.” The thread numbers carry little information in async code, because a task can run on a different thread after every await. What matters is that the two stacks show two tasks touching the same memory without isolation between them.

The fix follows from the location. The heap block allocated in async_Main of size 24 is the SessionCache instance; the variable inside it is storage. The global is hits.

Fixing it, and confirming the fix

Both races go away when the state gets real protection:

import Synchronization

/// Sendable because its state is protected, so no @unchecked is needed.
final class SessionCache: Sendable {
    private let storage = Mutex<[String: Int]>([:])

    func record(_ key: String) {
        storage.withLock { $0[key, default: 0] += 1 }
    }

    var count: Int {
        storage.withLock { $0.count }
    }
}

let hits = Mutex(0)

@concurrent
func hammer(_ cache: SessionCache) async {
    await withTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
        for worker in 0..<4 {
            group.addTask {
                for request in 0..<200 {
                    cache.record("key-\((worker * 200 + request) % 50)")
                    hits.withLock { $0 += 1 }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

let cache = SessionCache()
await hammer(cache)
assert(cache.count == 50)
assert(hits.withLock { $0 } == 800, "No increment was lost")

Run under TSan, this version produced no warnings and exited normally, with all 800 increments counted. Removing @unchecked from the class was part of the fix, not a side effect: with the state in a Mutex, the compiler verifies the Sendable conformance, so the next edit that adds an unprotected var will not compile.

The same program written with an actor instead of a Mutex, eight tasks each making 1,000 calls to an actor’s increment(), also ran without a single report and produced the exact count of 8,000. That is TSan confirming that the runtime’s actor and task synchronization establish the happens-before edges it needs.

Where TSan earns its keep in Swift 6 code

Swift 6’s static checking means TSan finds fewer races than it did in Swift 5 code, and finds them in predictable places. Focus test runs under TSan on code that contains:

  • @unchecked Sendable types. Each is a claim about synchronization the compiler did not verify. TSan verifies it for the paths your tests exercise.
  • nonisolated(unsafe) declarations. Same claim, applied to a variable.
  • Modules in Swift 5 mode and @preconcurrency imports, where diagnostics are downgraded or suppressed.
  • Objective-C, C, and C++ code, including callbacks from C libraries into Swift.
  • Unsafe pointers and manually managed memory shared between threads.
  • Code that hands closures to GCD or other non-Swift-concurrency APIs, where the isolation inference rules described in the threads article apply.

TSan does not find logic races, such as the stale results and reentrancy bugs earlier in this series, because those involve properly synchronized accesses in the wrong order. For those, use the controlled interleaving techniques from the testing article.

What it costs

TSan instruments every memory access and keeps shadow state for every location. For the race-free actor version of the workload above, 8,000 actor calls across eight tasks, on the test machine:

Build Wall time Peak memory
Without TSan 0.01 s 6.5 MB
With TSan 2.1 s 57 MB

This workload is a near worst case: almost nothing but synchronization, which TSan instruments heavily, plus its fixed start-up cost. LLVM’s documentation describes typical overhead as a slowdown of about 5 to 15 times and memory usage 5 to 10 times higher. Either way, TSan is a testing tool, not something to leave enabled in everyday development builds of a large app.

Making it routine

  • Run the test suite under TSan regularly, nightly or on every merge to the main branch, not only when someone suspects a race. Races found long after they were introduced are much harder to fix.
  • Write tests that create concurrency. TSan can only report races that happen. A test that calls record from one task proves nothing; the test above calls it from four at once, many times. Stress loops sized as in the continuation ownership article work well here.
  • Treat every report as a bug. Do not suppress reports in your own code. Suppression files exist for third-party code you cannot fix, and each entry should name the issue tracking the fix upstream.
  • Fail the build on reports. Set TSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1 in CI to stop at the first report, which keeps logs short and makes failures unambiguous.
  • Rerun with an optimized build occasionally. Some races only manifest when code runs fast enough for the accesses to overlap.

TSan and exclusivity enforcement

Swift also checks one related property without any sanitizer: exclusive access. Swift requires that a variable not be modified while another access to it is in progress, and the runtime enforces this for class properties, globals, and escaping closure captures in both debug and release builds. A violation stops the program with “Simultaneous accesses to …, but modification requires exclusive access.” Exclusivity checking is aimed at overlapping accesses within one thread, such as passing the same property as two inout arguments. It is not a race detector. When two threads conflict it may catch the overlap or may not, depending on timing; TSan catches it reliably whenever the two accesses execute without synchronization.

Summary

  • Swift 6 proves race freedom for checked code. TSan finds races at run time in the code behind escape hatches: @unchecked Sendable, nonisolated(unsafe), Swift 5 mode modules, @preconcurrency, and C or Objective-C.
  • TSan uses vector clocks to detect conflicting accesses without happens-before ordering. It reports races that happen in a run, even if the result happened to be correct.
  • Enable it in the scheme’s Diagnostics, or with --sanitize=thread. It runs on macOS and simulators, not on devices.
  • Reports show two stacks, the memory location, and the threads. In async code, frames are partial functions and threads matter less than tasks.
  • On the test machine, a cleanly compiling program produced seven reports and lost 60 of 800 increments; the Mutex and actor versions produced none.
  • Overhead is large, here 200 times slower and 9 times the memory on a synchronization-heavy workload, so run TSan in tests and CI, not in everyday builds.

Exercise

Write a small ImageCache class backed by NSCache and a plain [URL: Date] dictionary for access times, mark it @unchecked Sendable, and use it from a task group that loads and evicts images concurrently. Run the tests under TSan and fix each report it finds. Then decide, for each piece of state, whether a Mutex, an actor, or NSCache’s own thread safety is the right protection, and remove the @unchecked.

Further reading

  • Diagnosing memory, thread, and crash issues early in Apple’s Xcode documentation.
  • The ThreadSanitizer documentation from the LLVM project, including supported options.
  • SE-0176: Enforce Exclusive Access to Memory.
  • Sendable in Swift, on when @unchecked Sendable is justified.

Previous: Avoiding Deadlocks and Blocking Waits. Next: Profiling Task Lifetimes and Main-Actor Contention.

Thread Sanitizer (TSan) checks the other way around: at run time, for the code paths a test actually executes. It instruments every memory access, tracks which accesses are ordered by synchronization, and reports any two conflicting accesses that are not. This article runs TSan on races that compile cleanly in Swift 6 mode, shows how to read its reports, measures its overhead, and describes how to make it a routine part of testing.

entry.title: Avoiding Deadlocks and Blocking Waits in Swift Concurrency

link.title: Avoiding Deadlocks and Blocking Waits in Swift Concurrency

entry.content:
Swift concurrency removes the most common way to deadlock: actors are reentrant, so two actors that call each other do not lock each other up, and Mutex.withLock cannot be held across an await. It does not remove deadlocks altogether. A program can still reach a state where every piece of work it needs is waiting for another piece of work that cannot run, and in async code that state is often quieter than a classic deadlock: no thread is stuck in a lock, the CPU is idle, and the app simply never finishes what it started.

This article reproduces the deadlocks that remain, each one safely, with a timeout instead of a hang: blocking the main thread on main-actor work, starving the cooperative pool with blocking waits, waiting on yourself, and cyclic waits between tasks. It then shows how to diagnose them, because a suspended task does not appear in a thread backtrace, and the habits that prevent them.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26, on a machine whose cooperative pool has 20 threads. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift. Mutex requires iOS 18, macOS 15, or later.

What a deadlock is

A deadlock is a cycle of waits: A waits for B, B waits for C, and something in the chain waits for A. Coffman, Elphick, and Shoshani identified four conditions that must all hold for one to occur: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait. Remove any one, and the deadlock cannot happen.

Swift concurrency attacks the conditions in specific places:

  • Actor reentrancy removes hold-and-wait for actors. An actor that suspends on an await releases itself, so it does not hold anything while it waits.
  • Mutex.withLock takes a synchronous closure, so a lock cannot be held while waiting on asynchronous work.
  • Structured concurrency makes most waits point downward, from parents to children, which cannot form a cycle.

The deadlocks that remain come from bringing blocking into async code, from unstructured or continuation-based waits that can point anywhere, and from synchronous locks used the classic way.

flowchart LR
    accTitle: A deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph
    A["Main thread, blocked on semaphore"] -- "waits for signal from" --> B["Task isolated to the main actor"]
    B -- "needs to run on" --> A
    C["20 pool threads, blocked on semaphore"] -- "wait for signal from" --> D["Signalling task"]
    D -- "needs a free thread from" --> C

Deadlock 1: the main thread waits for main-actor work

The most common deadlock in apps adopting Swift concurrency is a synchronous function on the main thread that starts async work and blocks until it finishes, typically to satisfy a synchronous API that must return a value:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

/// A blocking wait with a timeout, so these demonstrations report instead of hanging.
func blockingWait(on semaphore: DispatchSemaphore, milliseconds: Int) -> DispatchTimeoutResult {
    semaphore.wait(timeout: .now() + .milliseconds(milliseconds))
}

@MainActor
func synchronousAPIThatWaitsForAsyncWork() -> DispatchTimeoutResult {
    let done = DispatchSemaphore(value: 0)
    Task {                       // Inherits the main actor.
        done.signal()
    }
    return blockingWait(on: done, milliseconds: 300)
}

let mainActorResult = synchronousAPIThatWaitsForAsyncWork()
assert(mainActorResult == .timedOut, "The task needed the main actor, which was blocked waiting for it")

The task is isolated to the main actor, so it cannot start until the current main-actor job finishes. That job is the function waiting for it. With an untimed wait(), the app freezes permanently; the watchdog on iOS eventually kills it.

Swift 6 makes the direct form a compile error: DispatchSemaphore.wait() is unavailable from asynchronous contexts. But the wait here happens in a synchronous helper called from a synchronous function, and nothing in the type system objects. The rule the compiler cannot enforce is: never block a thread waiting for async work that may need that thread. If a synchronous API must return something only async code can produce, the API has to change, to async, to a completion handler, or to returning a placeholder and updating later.

Deadlock 2: starving the cooperative pool

The cooperative pool has a fixed width, as the threads article measured. If every pool thread blocks waiting for something that itself needs a pool thread, nothing can run:

let poolWidth = ProcessInfo.processInfo.activeProcessorCount

/// Starts `blockers` tasks that block until signalled, and one task that signals all of them.
func blockedWaiters(blockers: Int) async -> (succeeded: Int, timedOut: Int) {
    let signal = DispatchSemaphore(value: 0)
    return await withTaskGroup(of: DispatchTimeoutResult?.self) { group in
        for _ in 0..<blockers {
            group.addTask { blockingWait(on: signal, milliseconds: 400) }
        }
        group.addTask {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))
            for _ in 0..<blockers { signal.signal() }
            return nil
        }
        var succeeded = 0
        var timedOut = 0
        for await result in group {
            switch result {
            case .success?: succeeded += 1
            case .timedOut?: timedOut += 1
            case nil: break
            }
        }
        return (succeeded, timedOut)
    }
}

let starved = await blockedWaiters(blockers: poolWidth)
let notStarved = await blockedWaiters(blockers: poolWidth - 1)
assert(starved == (0, poolWidth), "Every pool thread blocked; the signalling task never ran")
assert(notStarved == (poolWidth - 1, 0), "One free thread was enough for the signaller")
print("pool width \(poolWidth): \(starved) with \(poolWidth) blockers, \(notStarved) with one fewer")

With 20 blocked tasks on a 20-thread pool, all 20 timed out: the signalling task was runnable the whole time, and no thread was free to run it. With 19, the signaller found the twentieth thread and released everyone. The condition is exactly

\[B \ge W \quad\text{and}\quad \text{the releasing work needs the pool} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{deadlock},\]

where \(B\) is the number of pool threads blocked and \(W\) is the pool width. In production, \(W\) is the device’s core count, so this deadlock appears on a six-core phone with six blocked tasks, and not on a twenty-core development machine with six. It is the definition of a bug that “only happens on some devices.”

The fix is to wait without blocking. An async signal, built on continuations, suspends its waiters and frees their threads:

/// Suspends waiters until signalled. Waiting costs no thread.
actor AsyncSignal {
    private var signalled = false
    private var waiters: [CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>] = []

    func wait() async {
        guard !signalled else { return }
        await withCheckedContinuation { waiters.append($0) }
    }

    func signal() {
        signalled = true
        for waiter in waiters { waiter.resume() }
        waiters.removeAll()
    }
}

let asyncSignal = AsyncSignal()
let clock = ContinuousClock()
let asyncStart = clock.now
await withTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
    for _ in 0..<(poolWidth * 10) {
        group.addTask { await asyncSignal.wait() }
    }
    group.addTask {
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))
        await asyncSignal.signal()
    }
}
let asyncElapsed = asyncStart.duration(to: clock.now)
assert(asyncElapsed < .milliseconds(200), "Ten times the pool width of waiters, released promptly")

Two hundred waiters on a twenty-thread pool were released about 20 ms after the signal. None of them held a thread while waiting.

Deadlock 3: waiting on yourself

An operation that waits for something only it can produce never finishes. In async code the shape is usually indirect: a serializer that runs operations one at a time, and an operation that, somewhere deep in its call graph, submits more work to the same serializer and awaits it.

/// Runs operations one at a time, each after the previous one finishes.
actor SerialQueue {
    private var tail: Task<Void, Never>?

    func run<T: Sendable>(_ operation: @escaping @Sendable () async -> T) async -> T {
        let previous = tail
        let current = Task {
            await previous?.value
            return await operation()
        }
        tail = Task { _ = await current.value }
        return await current.value
    }
}

let finished = Mutex(false)
let serial = SerialQueue()
let selfWaiting = Task {
    _ = await serial.run {
        // A nested call on the same queue: it waits for the outer operation, which waits for it.
        await serial.run { 42 }
    }
    finished.withLock { $0 = true }
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(200))
assert(!finished.withLock { $0 }, "The nested operation waits for the outer one forever")
selfWaiting.cancel()        // Cancellation does not help: nothing in the cycle checks for it.

The nested run is queued behind the outer operation, and the outer operation is waiting for the nested one to return. Cancelling the task does nothing, because neither side is at a cancellable suspension point: each is awaiting a task’s value, which waits for completion regardless of cancellation. The task above stays suspended until the process exits.

This is precisely the deadlock that actor reentrancy was designed to avoid, as the actor reentrancy article explains, reintroduced by building a non-reentrant section on top of actors. It also appears with DispatchQueue.sync called on the queue you are already running on, where GCD detects it and crashes rather than hanging, and with MainActor code that synchronously waits on a main-queue sync call.

Prefer designs that do not need a non-reentrant section. If you must have one, make it detect re-entry: record a task-local marker while inside, and fail loudly when run is called with the marker already set.

Deadlock 4: cyclic waits between tasks

Unstructured tasks can wait on each other in any shape. Two tasks that each await the other’s value form the smallest cycle:

final class HandleStore: Sendable {
    let first = Mutex<Task<Int, Never>?>(nil)
    let second = Mutex<Task<Int, Never>?>(nil)
}

let handles = HandleStore()
let cycleFinished = Mutex(0)
handles.first.withLock { slot in
    slot = Task {
        while handles.second.withLock({ $0 }) == nil { await Task.yield() }
        let other = await handles.second.withLock { $0 }!.value
        cycleFinished.withLock { $0 += 1 }
        return other + 1
    }
}
handles.second.withLock { slot in
    slot = Task {
        let other = await handles.first.withLock { $0 }!.value
        cycleFinished.withLock { $0 += 1 }
        return other + 1
    }
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(200))
assert(cycleFinished.withLock { $0 } == 0, "Each task waits for the other; neither can finish")

Real cycles are rarely this direct. They form through caches that share in-flight loads, like the one in the actor reentrancy article: if loading A requires B, and loading B requires A, both callers join each other’s in-flight task and wait forever. Structured concurrency prevents such cycles by construction, since a parent waits only for its own children. Unstructured tasks and shared in-flight work need an explicit rule: a dependency graph that is known to be acyclic, or a check that refuses to join a load already on the current call path.

Deadlock 5: lock ordering in synchronous code

Synchronous locks still deadlock the classic way. If one code path takes lock A then lock B, and another takes B then A, two threads can each hold one lock and wait for the other. Swift’s Mutex makes this harder to write by accident, because the nested lock must appear lexically inside the outer withLock closure, but not impossible.

The standard rules still apply:

  • Do not nest locks. Copy what you need out of one critical section before entering another.
  • If you must nest, impose a global order, such as by object identity or a documented hierarchy, and acquire in that order everywhere.
  • Never call unknown code while holding a lock. Resuming a continuation, calling a delegate, or invoking a closure from inside withLock can re-enter the lock or take another one. Every example in this series takes the continuation out under the lock and resumes it after.

Diagnosing a hang

Classic deadlocks are visible in a debugger: pause the app, and two threads are blocked in __psynch_mutexwait or semaphore_wait_trap, each holding what the other wants. Async deadlocks are different, and the difference is the most useful thing to know when debugging one.

Symptom Likely cause Where to look
Main thread blocked in a semaphore or lock wait Deadlock 1, or a lock held too long Xcode’s debug navigator; the main thread’s backtrace
All pool threads blocked in semaphore waits, nothing progressing Deadlock 2 Backtraces of threads named after the cooperative queue
Threads idle, CPU idle, work never completes Deadlocks 3 and 4, or a leaked continuation Task-level tools, not thread backtraces
SWIFT TASK CONTINUATION MISUSE ... leaked its continuation in the console A continuation dropped without resuming The function named in the message

The third row is the hard one. A suspended task does not occupy a thread, so it does not appear in any thread’s backtrace. Pausing the app shows idle threads and nothing obviously wrong. To see it, you need tools that show tasks:

  • Instruments’ Swift Tasks instrument records every task’s state over time, including tasks that are suspended and never resume. Named tasks, created with Task(name:) in Swift 6.2, are far easier to find. The profiling article walks through it.
  • Continuation misuse messages catch leaked checked continuations when they are destroyed.
  • swift-inspect, a command-line tool shipped with the toolchain, can dump the tasks and actors of a running process when it is allowed to attach to it, as with debug builds.
  • Timeouts in tests. A test with .timeLimit turns a silent hang into a failure that points at the operation that never completed, as the controlled interleavings article recommends.

Habits that prevent deadlocks

  1. Never block in async code, or on a thread that async code may need. Not with semaphores, not with DispatchGroup.wait, not with Thread.sleep, and not indirectly through a synchronous helper.
  2. Keep waits structured. Parents awaiting children cannot form cycles. Be suspicious of every unstructured task that awaits another unstructured task.
  3. Do not build non-reentrant sections on top of actors unless re-entry is detected and rejected.
  4. Make shared in-flight work acyclic. Know the dependency graph of anything that joins other callers’ work.
  5. Do not nest synchronous locks, and never resume continuations or call out while holding one.
  6. Name long-lived tasks and bound tests in time, so the hangs you do get are diagnosable.

Summary

  • Swift concurrency removes the classic actor-to-actor deadlock through reentrancy, and lock-across-await through Mutex’s synchronous API.
  • Blocking the main thread on main-actor work deadlocks; Swift 6 catches only the direct form.
  • Blocking pool threads deadlocks when \(B \ge W\) blocked threads wait for work that needs the pool. On the test machine, 20 blockers deadlocked and 19 did not. Async signals avoid it entirely.
  • Non-reentrant serializers and cyclic waits between unstructured tasks hang silently, and cancellation does not break the cycle.
  • Synchronous locks still need the classic discipline: no nesting, or a global order, and no calling out while held.
  • Async hangs show idle threads. Diagnose them with task-level tools, continuation misuse messages, and time-limited tests.

Exercise

Write a ConfigLoader actor that loads configuration files, where a file may include other files, and concurrent loads of the same file share one in-flight task. Construct two files that include each other and show that the naive design hangs. Then add cycle detection: track the chain of files being loaded in a task-local value, and throw a descriptive error when a load would join a file already in the chain. Test both the cycle and a diamond-shaped include graph, which must still share work without reporting a false cycle.

Further reading

  • Coffman, Elphick, and Shoshani, System Deadlocks, ACM Computing Surveys, 1971.
  • Swift concurrency: Behind the scenes, WWDC21, on the forward-progress contract.
  • SE-0340: Unavailable From Async Attribute, which makes the most common blocking calls compile errors in async code.

Previous: Testing Concurrent Work with Controlled Interleavings. Next: Finding Data Races with Thread Sanitizer.

entry.title: Testing Concurrent Swift Code with Controlled Interleavings

link.title: Testing Concurrent Swift Code with Controlled Interleavings

entry.content:
A concurrent test that sleeps is a test that guesses. It guesses how long the work takes on the machine it happens to run on, under whatever load that machine happens to have. Guess short and the test fails at random on a busy CI runner. Guess long and the suite gets slow, and still fails occasionally, because no fixed duration is enough for every run.

The alternative is to take control of the three things that make concurrent behavior nondeterministic: when work finishes, where it pauses, and what time it is. A test that awaits work instead of sleeping, holds operations at chosen suspension points, and advances a clock of its own can reproduce a specific interleaving every time, in microseconds. This article builds those tools, a gate, a manual test clock, and a bounded condition wait, and uses them with Swift Testing to test a debounced search model under interleavings that would otherwise appear only in production.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and the Swift Testing framework, and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. The production code builds on itself in one module; the tests were run with swift test in a package containing that module. Mutex requires iOS 18, macOS 15, or later. The earlier Testing Asynchronous Swift Code article covers the XCTest side of the same ideas.

Why sleeping tests fail, quantitatively

Suppose a test starts an operation, sleeps for \(d\), then checks the result. If the operation’s duration \(L\) on a given run is random, the test fails whenever \(L > d\). Even a well-behaved distribution has a tail. If \(L\) is exponential with mean \(m\):

\[P(\text{flake}) = P(L > d) = e^{-d/m}, \qquad d = m \ln\frac{1}{P(\text{flake})}.\]

To keep one test’s flake rate at 0.1%, it must sleep \(m \ln 1000 \approx 6.9\,m\): almost seven times the average duration, every run. A suite of 500 such tests, each at 0.1%, fails at least once in \(1 - 0.999^{500} \approx 39\%\) of runs. Real CI latency distributions have heavier tails than the exponential, so the real numbers are worse. Sleeping makes a suite both slow and unreliable, and there is no value of \(d\) that fixes it.

The fix is structural: make the test know when things happen rather than guess.

flowchart LR
    accTitle: A test controls completion, suspension, and time through injected dependencies
    T["Test"] -- "await model.settle()" --> M["Model under test"]
    T -- "open gate for query" --> G["Gated backend"]
    T -- "advance(by:)" --> C["Test clock"]
    M -- "search(query)" --> G
    M -- "sleep(for: quietPeriod)" --> C
    G -. "holds each request until opened" .-> M
    C -. "wakes sleepers only when advanced" .-> M

Tool 1: await the work, not the clock

The simplest control is to give the test something to await. A model that starts unstructured tasks should expose a way to wait for them, as every model in this series has with settle(). Tests then await completion directly:

model.queryChanged("swift")
await model.settle()
#expect(model.results == ["swift result"])

This removes the guess about when work finishes. It does not control what happens in between, which is where the interesting bugs live.

Tool 2: gates that hold operations mid-flight

A gate is a dependency that suspends until the test opens it. Injected into a fake backend, it lets the test hold a request at the network boundary while other things happen:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

/// Suspends callers until opened.
actor Gate {
    private var isOpen = false
    private var waiters: [CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>] = []

    func wait() async {
        guard !isOpen else { return }
        await withCheckedContinuation { waiters.append($0) }
    }

    func open() {
        isOpen = true
        for waiter in waiters { waiter.resume() }
        waiters.removeAll()
    }
}

protocol SearchBackend: Sendable {
    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [String]
}

/// A fake backend that records each request and holds it until the test opens that query's gate.
final class GatedBackend: SearchBackend {
    private let state = Mutex<(requests: [String], gates: [String: Gate])>(([], [:]))

    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [String] {
        let gate = state.withLock { state -> Gate in
            state.requests.append(query)
            if let existing = state.gates[query] { return existing }
            let gate = Gate()
            state.gates[query] = gate
            return gate
        }
        await gate.wait()
        return ["\(query) result"]
    }

    func release(_ query: String) async {
        let gate = state.withLock { state -> Gate in
            if let existing = state.gates[query] { return existing }
            let gate = Gate()
            state.gates[query] = gate
            return gate
        }
        await gate.open()
    }

    var requests: [String] {
        state.withLock { $0.requests }
    }
}

With a gate per query, the test decides the order in which responses arrive. That is the order the stale results article had to simulate with carefully chosen latencies; here it is a line of test code.

Tool 3: a clock the test controls

Debouncing, timeouts, retries with backoff, polling intervals: any code that waits for time is untestable at speed unless time itself is a dependency. Swift’s Clock protocol (SE-0329) makes it one. Production code takes some Clock<Duration> and calls clock.sleep(for:); tests pass a clock that moves only when advanced.

The test clock below is careful about cancellation. A debounced model cancels its sleeping task on every keystroke, so the clock’s sleepers must be removed when cancelled, including when cancellation arrives before the sleeper has registered. It uses the same phase-per-waiter design as the permit pool in the cancellation handlers article:

/// A clock that moves only when a test advances it.
final class TestClock: Clock, Sendable {
    struct Instant: InstantProtocol {
        let offset: Duration

        func advanced(by duration: Duration) -> Instant {
            Instant(offset: offset + duration)
        }

        func duration(to other: Instant) -> Duration {
            other.offset - offset
        }

        static func < (lhs: Instant, rhs: Instant) -> Bool {
            lhs.offset < rhs.offset
        }
    }

    private enum Phase {
        case registering
        case waiting(deadline: Instant, continuation: CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>)
        case cancelledEarly
    }

    private struct State {
        var now = Instant(offset: .zero)
        var phases: [UInt64: Phase] = [:]
        var nextID: UInt64 = 0
    }

    private let state = Mutex(State())

    var now: Instant {
        state.withLock { $0.now }
    }

    var minimumResolution: Duration {
        .zero
    }

    func sleep(until deadline: Instant, tolerance: Duration? = nil) async throws {
        let id = state.withLock { state -> UInt64 in
            state.nextID += 1
            state.phases[state.nextID] = .registering
            return state.nextID
        }
        try await withTaskCancellationHandler {
            try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { (continuation: CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>) in
                enum Decision { case resumeNow, cancelNow, wait }
                let decision = state.withLock { state -> Decision in
                    if case .cancelledEarly = state.phases[id] {
                        state.phases[id] = nil
                        return .cancelNow
                    }
                    if deadline <= state.now {
                        state.phases[id] = nil
                        return .resumeNow
                    }
                    state.phases[id] = .waiting(deadline: deadline, continuation: continuation)
                    return .wait
                }
                switch decision {
                case .resumeNow: continuation.resume()
                case .cancelNow: continuation.resume(throwing: CancellationError())
                case .wait: break
                }
            }
        } onCancel: {
            let sleeper = state.withLock { state -> CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>? in
                switch state.phases[id] {
                case .registering:
                    state.phases[id] = .cancelledEarly
                    return nil
                case .waiting(_, let continuation):
                    state.phases[id] = nil
                    return continuation
                case .cancelledEarly, nil:
                    return nil
                }
            }
            sleeper?.resume(throwing: CancellationError())
        }
    }

    /// Moves time forward and wakes, in deadline order, every sleeper that is now due.
    func advance(by duration: Duration) {
        let due = state.withLock { state -> [CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>] in
            state.now = state.now.advanced(by: duration)
            var due: [(deadline: Instant, id: UInt64, continuation: CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>)] = []
            for (id, phase) in state.phases {
                if case .waiting(let deadline, let continuation) = phase, deadline <= state.now {
                    due.append((deadline, id, continuation))
                    state.phases[id] = nil
                }
            }
            return due.sorted { ($0.deadline, $0.id) < ($1.deadline, $1.id) }.map(\.continuation)
        }
        for continuation in due {
            continuation.resume()
        }
    }

    /// The number of sleepers currently waiting for time to advance.
    var sleeperCount: Int {
        state.withLock { state in
            state.phases.values.filter { phase in
                if case .waiting = phase { true } else { false }
            }.count
        }
    }
}

Sleepers due at the same deadline wake in registration order, so tests that advance past several deadlines see a deterministic order. sleeperCount lets a test wait until the code under test has actually reached its sleep before advancing, which is the step most hand-rolled test clocks forget.

Tool 4: wait for conditions, with a bound

Sometimes the test must wait for a background effect that no handle exposes, such as a request reaching the backend or a sleeper registering with the clock. Polling a condition with Task.yield() waits exactly as long as needed. A real-time bound turns a bug that would hang the test into a failure with a message:

/// Yields until `condition` holds. Returns false after `limit` of real time instead of hanging.
nonisolated(nonsending)
func waitUntil(_ limit: Duration = .seconds(2), _ condition: () async -> Bool) async -> Bool {
    let clock = ContinuousClock()
    let deadline = clock.now + limit
    while clock.now < deadline {
        if await condition() { return true }
        await Task.yield()
    }
    return await condition()
}

The limit is not a sleep: a passing test never waits for it. It only bounds how long a failing test takes to report. nonisolated(nonsending) lets the condition closure read main-actor state when the test runs on the main actor, as the isolated and nonisolated article explains.

The code under test

The model is the debounced search from the stale results article, rewritten to take its clock and backend as dependencies:

@MainActor
final class SearchViewModel<C: Clock<Duration>> {
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private(set) var isSearching = false
    private var current: Task<Void, Never>?
    private var generation = 0
    private let clock: C
    private let backend: any SearchBackend
    private let quietPeriod: Duration

    init(clock: C, backend: any SearchBackend, quietPeriod: Duration = .milliseconds(80)) {
        self.clock = clock
        self.backend = backend
        self.quietPeriod = quietPeriod
    }

    func queryChanged(_ query: String) {
        generation += 1
        let requestGeneration = generation
        current?.cancel()
        current = Task {
            do {
                try await clock.sleep(for: quietPeriod)
            } catch {
                return
            }
            isSearching = true
            defer {
                if requestGeneration == generation { isSearching = false }
            }
            guard let found = try? await backend.search(query), requestGeneration == generation else { return }
            results = found
        }
    }

    func settle() async {
        await current?.value
    }
}

In production it is created with ContinuousClock(); in tests with TestClock(). Nothing else about it knows it is being tested.

Test: debouncing waits for the quiet period

import Testing

@MainActor
@Test(.timeLimit(.minutes(1)))
func debounceIssuesOneRequestAfterTheQuietPeriod() async {
    let clock = TestClock()
    let backend = GatedBackend()
    let model = SearchViewModel(clock: clock, backend: backend)

    for query in ["s", "sw", "swi", "swif", "swift"] {
        model.queryChanged(query)
    }
    #expect(await waitUntil { clock.sleeperCount == 1 }, "Only the latest keystroke is still waiting")

    clock.advance(by: .milliseconds(79))
    #expect(backend.requests.isEmpty, "Nothing is sent before the quiet period ends")

    clock.advance(by: .milliseconds(1))
    #expect(await waitUntil { backend.requests == ["swift"] })
    #expect(model.isSearching)

    await backend.release("swift")
    await model.settle()
    #expect(model.results == ["swift result"])
    #expect(!model.isSearching)
}

This test runs in about a millisecond and checks the debounce to the millisecond: nothing at 79 ms, exactly one request at 80 ms, for the last query only. A sleep-based version would need real 80 ms waits, and could not distinguish 79 from 80 at all.

Test: every arrival order gives the same answer

The stale-result bug depends on the order responses arrive. With gates, the test enumerates the orders instead of hoping to hit the bad one, and Swift Testing’s parameterized tests run each as a separate case:

@MainActor
@Test(arguments: [["first", "second"], ["second", "first"]])
func newestQueryWinsInEveryArrivalOrder(releaseOrder: [String]) async {
    let clock = TestClock()
    let backend = GatedBackend()
    let model = SearchViewModel(clock: clock, backend: backend)

    model.queryChanged("first")
    #expect(await waitUntil { clock.sleeperCount == 1 })
    clock.advance(by: .milliseconds(80))
    #expect(await waitUntil { backend.requests == ["first"] })

    model.queryChanged("second")
    #expect(await waitUntil { clock.sleeperCount == 1 })
    clock.advance(by: .milliseconds(80))
    #expect(await waitUntil { backend.requests == ["first", "second"] })

    for query in releaseOrder {
        await backend.release(query)
        await Task.yield()
    }
    await model.settle()
    #expect(await waitUntil { !model.isSearching })
    #expect(model.results == ["second result"], "Released in order \(releaseOrder)")
}

Both requests are in flight at the same time, a situation the debounce normally prevents and the test creates deliberately. Each case then releases them in a different order. The generation check makes the newest query win in both. Removing the check, which is the kind of “cleanup” a refactor might do, makes the ["second", "first"] case fail deterministically on every run.

For two operations there are two orders. For \(n\) independent completions there are \(n!\), which grows too fast to enumerate beyond four or five. At that point, combine targeted cases for the orders you reason are dangerous with seeded random stress runs, sized with the formula from the continuation ownership article.

Test: events delivered through callbacks

Some behavior is observable only through a callback: a delegate method, a closure property, a notification. Swift Testing’s confirmation turns “this callback must be called exactly N times” into an assertion, without sleeping:

@Test
func backendRecordsEveryRequestExactlyOnce() async throws {
    let backend = GatedBackend()
    try await confirmation("each search returns", expectedCount: 3) { searchReturned in
        try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
            for query in ["a", "b", "c"] {
                group.addTask {
                    _ = try await backend.search(query)
                    searchReturned()
                }
            }
            for query in ["c", "a", "b"] {
                await backend.release(query)
            }
            try await group.waitForAll()
        }
    }
    #expect(backend.requests.sorted() == ["a", "b", "c"])
}

confirmation fails the test if the closure it provides is called fewer or more times than expectedCount by the time its body returns. The body must therefore wait for the events itself, here by awaiting the task group. A confirmation is a count, not a timer.

Running concurrent tests reliably

A few practices keep concurrent suites deterministic as they grow:

  • Inject every source of nondeterminism. Clocks, backends, random generators, and UUID sources. If a test cannot control it, the test cannot pin it down.
  • Prefer waitUntil on a condition over Task.sleep for a duration. A bounded condition wait never makes a passing test slower.
  • Bound every test in time. .timeLimit(.minutes(1)) turns a hang, usually a leaked continuation or a gate nobody opened, into a failure.
  • Run tests in parallel, and on purpose. Swift Testing runs tests in parallel by default, which is a free stress test for shared state between tests. Use .serialized only for suites that share an external resource, and treat a test that fails only in parallel as a bug report about hidden shared state.
  • Repeat suspicious tests. A test that has ever flaked should be run in a loop locally, a few hundred times, before and after the fix.
  • Run under Thread Sanitizer periodically. Controlled interleavings find logic races; Thread Sanitizer finds memory races in code that escapes Swift’s static checks.

Summary

  • Sleeping tests trade speed for reliability and get neither: a 0.1% flake rate needs about \(6.9\times\) the mean duration, and suites multiply flake rates.
  • Await completion directly through handles such as settle().
  • Hold operations at chosen suspension points with gates injected into fake dependencies.
  • Make time a dependency with Clock, and drive it in tests with a manual clock that handles cancellation and reports its sleepers.
  • Wait for conditions with a bounded yield loop rather than fixed sleeps.
  • Enumerate dangerous orderings with parameterized tests; use seeded stress runs when orderings explode combinatorially.
  • Use confirmation for callback counts and .timeLimit to turn hangs into failures.

Exercise

Add retry with exponential backoff to SearchViewModel: on failure, wait 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms, before giving up. Write Swift Testing tests that use TestClock to verify the exact retry schedule, that a new query during a backoff wait cancels the pending retry, and that a success on the second attempt stops further retries. None of the tests should take more than a few milliseconds of real time.

Further reading

  • Swift Testing documentation, including confirmation and traits.
  • SE-0329: Clock, Instant, and Duration and SE-0374: Add sleep(for:) to Clock.
  • Meet Swift Testing and Go further with Swift Testing, WWDC24.
  • Testing Asynchronous Swift Code, the XCTest-based companion article.
