entry.summary: A concurrent test that sleeps is a test that guesses. It guesses how long the work takes on the machine it happens to run on, under whatever load that machine happens to have. Guess short and the test fails at random on a busy CI runner. Guess long and the suite gets slow, and still fails occasionally, because no fixed duration is enough for every run. The alternative is to take control of the three things that make concurrent behavior nondeterministic: when work finishes, where it pauses, and what time it is. A test that awaits work instead of sleeping, holds operations at chosen suspension points, and advances a clock of its own can reproduce a specific interleaving every time, in microseconds. This article builds those tools, a gate, a manual test clock, and a bounded condition wait, and uses them with Swift Testing to test a debounced search model under interleavings that would otherwise appear only in production.

entry.title: Rejecting Stale Results After Request Replacement in Swift

link.title: Rejecting Stale Results After Request Replacement in Swift

entry.content:
A user types “swift” into a search field. Five requests go out, one per keystroke. The response for “s” is large and slow; the response for “swift” is small and fast. “swift” arrives first and is displayed. Then “s” arrives and replaces it. The screen now shows results for a query the user typed a second ago and has since extended four times.

This is the stale-result bug, and it appears wherever a newer request replaces an older one: search fields, filters, pagination after a sort change, detail screens when the selection changes, map tiles when the viewport moves. Swift 6’s data-race checking does not catch it, because nothing races in the memory-model sense; the main actor applies each result in turn, in the wrong order. This article quantifies how often the reordering happens, then builds up the defenses in order: cancellation, generation tokens for results that arrive outside the task, commit checks for multi-step updates, and debouncing.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift. Mutex requires iOS 18, macOS 15, or later.

How often responses overtake each other

Suppose keystrokes are \(\Delta\) apart and request latencies are independent and exponentially distributed with mean \(m\), a common first model for network response times. Request \(i\) is sent at time \(t\) and request \(i+1\) at \(t + \Delta\). The older response arrives after the newer one when \(L_i > \Delta + L_{i+1}\). Integrating over \(L_{i+1}\):

\[P(\text{reorder}) = \int_0^\infty e^{-(\Delta + x)/m}\,\frac{1}{m}e^{-x/m}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\,e^{-\Delta/m}.\]

With a typing gap of 150 ms and a mean latency of 300 ms, \(P = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-0.5} \approx 0.30\): almost a third of consecutive request pairs arrive out of order. On a fast connection with a mean latency of 50 ms, \(P \approx 0.025\), rare enough to escape testing on office Wi-Fi and common enough to appear daily on cellular networks.

The formula is easy to check by simulation:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

struct SplitMix64: RandomNumberGenerator {
    private var state: UInt64

    init(seed: UInt64) {
        state = seed
    }

    mutating func next() -> UInt64 {
        state &+= 0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15
        var z = state
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) &* 0xBF58_476D_1CE4_E5B9
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) &* 0x94D0_49BB_1331_11EB
        return z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

func exponential(mean: Double, using generator: inout SplitMix64) -> Double {
    -mean * log(1 - Double.random(in: 0..<1, using: &generator))
}

func simulatedReorderRate(gap: Double, meanLatency: Double, trials: Int) -> Double {
    var generator = SplitMix64(seed: 42)
    var reordered = 0
    for _ in 0..<trials {
        let older = exponential(mean: meanLatency, using: &generator)
        let newer = exponential(mean: meanLatency, using: &generator)
        if older > gap + newer { reordered += 1 }
    }
    return Double(reordered) / Double(trials)
}

let predicted = 0.5 * exp(-150.0 / 300.0)
let simulated = simulatedReorderRate(gap: 150, meanLatency: 300, trials: 200_000)
assert(abs(simulated - predicted) < 0.01)
print("reorder probability: predicted \(predicted), simulated \(simulated)")

The simulation agreed with the formula to within a few thousandths. Real latency distributions have heavier tails than the exponential, which makes reordering more likely, not less: one slow response can overtake many fast ones.

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: An older, slower response overwrites the newer result
    participant U as Search field
    participant M as Model on the main actor
    participant S as Server
    U->>M: query "s"
    M->>S: search "s", slow
    U->>M: query "swift"
    M->>S: search "swift", fast
    S-->>M: results for "swift"
    M->>U: show "swift" results
    S-->>M: results for "s"
    M->>U: show "s" results, stale

A controllable fake service

The examples use a search service whose latency per query is set by the test, so every interleaving is deterministic:

final class SearchService: Sendable {
    private let latencies: [String: Duration]
    private let requests = Mutex<[String]>([])

    init(latencies: [String: Duration]) {
        self.latencies = latencies
    }

    /// Async API.
    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [String] {
        requests.withLock { $0.append(query) }
        try await Task.sleep(for: latencies[query] ?? .milliseconds(10))
        return ["\(query) result"]
    }

    /// Legacy callback API for the same backend. There is no handle to cancel.
    func search(_ query: String, completion: @escaping @Sendable ([String]) -> Void) {
        requests.withLock { $0.append(query) }
        let latency = latencies[query] ?? .milliseconds(10)
        let milliseconds = Int(latency.components.seconds * 1_000) + Int(latency.components.attoseconds / 1_000_000_000_000_000)
        DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + .milliseconds(milliseconds)) {
            completion(["\(query) result"])
        }
    }

    var requestLog: [String] {
        requests.withLock { $0 }
    }
}

/// The slow-first, fast-last shape that produces stale results.
let typingLatencies: [String: Duration] = [
    "s": .milliseconds(120), "sw": .milliseconds(90), "swi": .milliseconds(60),
    "swif": .milliseconds(30), "swift": .milliseconds(5),
]
let typedQueries = ["s", "sw", "swi", "swif", "swift"]

Step 0: the naive model

@MainActor
final class NaiveSearchModel {
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private var tasks: [Task<Void, Never>] = []
    private let service: SearchService

    init(service: SearchService) {
        self.service = service
    }

    func queryChanged(_ query: String) {
        tasks.append(Task {
            if let found = try? await service.search(query) {
                results = found
            }
        })
    }

    func settle() async {
        for task in tasks { await task.value }
    }
}

let naive = NaiveSearchModel(service: SearchService(latencies: typingLatencies))
for query in typedQueries {
    naive.queryChanged(query)
}
await naive.settle()
assert(naive.results == ["s result"], "The slowest, oldest response was applied last")

Every response was applied, in arrival order, and the oldest arrived last. Note that there is no data race here: the model is main-actor isolated, and every assignment is checked and serialized. The bug is entirely about which result wins.

Step 1: cancel the previous request

The first defense is to keep one handle and cancel it whenever a newer query arrives, checking for cancellation after the await and before committing:

@MainActor
final class CancellingSearchModel {
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private var current: Task<Void, Never>?
    private let service: SearchService

    init(service: SearchService) {
        self.service = service
    }

    func queryChanged(_ query: String) {
        current?.cancel()
        current = Task {
            guard let found = try? await service.search(query) else { return }
            guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            results = found
        }
    }

    func settle() async {
        await current?.value
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(150))      // Let any replaced task finish too.
    }
}

let cancelling = CancellingSearchModel(service: SearchService(latencies: typingLatencies))
for query in typedQueries {
    cancelling.queryChanged(query)
}
await cancelling.settle()
assert(cancelling.results == ["swift result"])

This version is correct for this shape, and it is worth understanding exactly why. The check and the assignment run on the main actor in one synchronous stretch, and cancel() is called from the main actor too. So no cancellation can arrive between the check and the assignment. A replaced task either sees the flag and returns, or was never replaced. Cancellation also saves work: Task.sleep, standing in for URLSession, stops early, so replaced requests stop consuming bandwidth.

The defense depends on three conditions: the work is a task you hold, its result is delivered through that task, and the commit happens in one isolated job after the check. When any of the three fails, cancellation is no longer sufficient.

Step 2: results that do not arrive through the task

A callback API has no task to cancel. The response arrives in a closure, whenever the server answers:

@MainActor
final class CallbackSearchModel {
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private let service: SearchService
    private var generation = 0
    let usesGeneration: Bool

    init(service: SearchService, usesGeneration: Bool) {
        self.service = service
        self.usesGeneration = usesGeneration
    }

    func queryChanged(_ query: String) {
        generation += 1
        let requestGeneration = generation
        service.search(query) { [weak self] found in
            Task { @MainActor in
                guard let self else { return }
                if self.usesGeneration, requestGeneration != self.generation {
                    return                              // A newer query has been issued since.
                }
                self.results = found
            }
        }
    }
}

let unguardedCallbacks = CallbackSearchModel(service: SearchService(latencies: typingLatencies), usesGeneration: false)
let guardedCallbacks = CallbackSearchModel(service: SearchService(latencies: typingLatencies), usesGeneration: true)
for query in typedQueries {
    unguardedCallbacks.queryChanged(query)
    guardedCallbacks.queryChanged(query)
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(200))
assert(unguardedCallbacks.results == ["s result"], "Without a token, the last response to arrive wins")
assert(guardedCallbacks.results == ["swift result"], "With a token, only the latest request may commit")

The generation token is a counter incremented for every new request. Each request captures the value current when it was issued, and its response may commit only if the counter has not moved since. Unlike the cancellation flag, the token is about identity: it does not ask “was this work cancelled?” but “is this still the request the user is waiting for?” It works for callbacks, for responses delivered through streams, for work shared between several callers, and for results produced by code you cannot cancel.

Tokens and cancellation are complementary. Cancellation stops work that is no longer wanted, saving bandwidth and battery. The token guarantees correctness regardless of whether the work stopped. A robust model uses both.

Step 3: multi-step commits

Some updates happen in stages: show the first page, then load thumbnails; show cached results, then refresh from the network; update the list, then the detail pane. Each stage is a separate commit after a separate await, and the request can be replaced between them. Check the token at every commit point:

@MainActor
final class StagedSearchModel {
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private(set) var details: [String: String] = [:]
    private(set) var appliedStages: [String] = []
    private var generation = 0
    private var current: Task<Void, Never>?
    private let service: SearchService

    init(service: SearchService) {
        self.service = service
    }

    func queryChanged(_ query: String) {
        generation += 1
        let requestGeneration = generation
        current?.cancel()
        current = Task {
            guard let found = try? await service.search(query), requestGeneration == generation else { return }
            results = found
            appliedStages.append("results for \(query)")

            try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(40))              // Second stage: load details.
            guard requestGeneration == generation else { return }
            details = Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: found.map { ($0, "details for \($0)") })
            appliedStages.append("details for \(query)")
        }
    }

    func settle() async {
        await current?.value
    }
}

let staged = StagedSearchModel(service: SearchService(latencies: ["first": .milliseconds(5), "second": .milliseconds(5)]))
staged.queryChanged("first")
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))          // "first" has shown results and is loading details.
staged.queryChanged("second")
await staged.settle()
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(60))
assert(staged.appliedStages == ["results for first", "results for second", "details for second"])
assert(staged.details.keys.sorted() == ["second result"], "The replaced request never applied its details")

The replaced request committed its first stage legitimately, then was replaced while loading details. The second check prevented it from writing details for “first” into a model that now shows results for “second”, a mismatch that would be visible as the wrong detail pane for the selected row.

Here, Task.sleep would also have thrown on cancellation, so the replaced task would have stopped anyway. The token check makes correctness independent of whether the second stage happens to be cancellable, which matters as soon as it is a legacy callback, a shared load, or a synchronous computation.

Step 4: fewer requests with debouncing

Every keystroke so far produced a request. Most of them were wasted. Debouncing waits until the input has been quiet for a short interval before starting work, and restarts the wait on every change. With tasks, a debounce is just a cancellable sleep at the start of the request:

@MainActor
final class DebouncedSearchModel {
    private(set) var results: [String] = []
    private var current: Task<Void, Never>?
    private var generation = 0
    private let service: SearchService
    private let quietPeriod: Duration

    init(service: SearchService, quietPeriod: Duration) {
        self.service = service
        self.quietPeriod = quietPeriod
    }

    func queryChanged(_ query: String) {
        generation += 1
        let requestGeneration = generation
        current?.cancel()
        current = Task {
            do {
                try await Task.sleep(for: quietPeriod)    // Cancelled by the next keystroke.
            } catch {
                return
            }
            guard let found = try? await service.search(query), requestGeneration == generation else { return }
            results = found
        }
    }

    func settle() async {
        await current?.value
    }
}

let debounceService = SearchService(latencies: typingLatencies)
let debounced = DebouncedSearchModel(service: debounceService, quietPeriod: .milliseconds(80))
for query in typedQueries {
    debounced.queryChanged(query)
    try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))      // Typing faster than the quiet period.
}
await debounced.settle()
assert(debounced.results == ["swift result"])
assert(debounceService.requestLog == ["swift"], "Five keystrokes, one request")

Five keystrokes produced one request. Debouncing does not replace the token: if the user pauses for longer than the quiet period and then keeps typing, two requests can be in flight, and the reordering analysis above applies again. It changes the effective gap \(\Delta\) in the formula to at least the quiet period, which lowers the reorder probability, \(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-\Delta/m}\), without eliminating it.

The quiet period is a trade-off between wasted requests and perceived latency. Values between 150 and 300 ms are typical for search; a filter that recomputes locally may not need debouncing at all.

In SwiftUI

SwiftUI’s .task(id:) modifier implements step 1 for you: when id changes, it cancels the running task and starts a new one. Combined with a quiet period inside the task, it also gives debouncing:

struct SearchView: View {
    @State private var query = ""
    @State private var results: [String] = []
    let service: SearchService

    var body: some View {
        List(results, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
            .searchable(text: $query)
            .task(id: query) {
                try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(200))
                guard !Task.isCancelled, let found = try? await service.search(query) else { return }
                results = found
            }
    }
}

The same three conditions apply. Because the work is a task SwiftUI holds, the result arrives through it, and the commit is a single main-actor assignment, the cancellation check is sufficient. Once the view model starts using callbacks, shared loaders, or multi-stage commits, add a token.

Summary

  • Replaced requests reorder often: with exponential latencies, \(P = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-\Delta/m}\), about 30% for a 150 ms typing gap and 300 ms mean latency.
  • The bug is not a data race; Swift 6 accepts it. It is about which result is allowed to commit.
  • Cancelling the previous task and checking Task.isCancelled before committing is sufficient when the work is a task you hold, its result comes through that task, and the commit is one isolated job.
  • Generation tokens make commits depend on request identity, so they also work for callbacks, streams, shared work, and uncancellable code.
  • Check the token at every commit point of a multi-stage update.
  • Debouncing removes most requests and widens the effective gap, but does not remove the need for a token.

Exercise

Build a PhotoGridModel whose visible range changes as the user scrolls. Each range change requests thumbnails for the new range through a shared ThumbnailLoader that deduplicates concurrent requests for the same photo, as in the task lifetime article. Because loads are shared, cancelling one range’s task must not cancel a thumbnail another range still needs. Use per-cell generation tokens so that a cell only shows the thumbnail for the photo it currently displays, and write a test that scrolls quickly back and forth across the same rows with randomized load latencies.

Further reading

  • Exponential distribution, for the latency model used above.
  • [task(id:name:priority:file:line::)](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/task(id:name:priority:file:line::)) in the SwiftUI documentation.
  • Discover concurrency in SwiftUI, WWDC21.

entry.title: Continuation Ownership, Cancellation, and Double Resume in Swift

link.title: Continuation Ownership, Cancellation, and Double Resume in Swift

entry.content:
A continuation wrapper is easy to write when exactly one thing can finish the operation. It becomes hard as soon as two things can: a completion handler and a cancellation, a response and a timeout, a success callback and a failure callback that a buggy SDK sometimes calls both of. Each of those pairs is a race to resume the same continuation, and the loser either crashes the process with a double resume or, if the wrapper is defensive in the wrong way, leaves the task suspended forever.

The way out is to treat a continuation as a resource with exactly one owner at any moment, and to make “who resumes” a single atomic decision. This article builds a small resolve-once primitive, uses it to make a cancellable legacy operation correct under three different cancellation contracts, adds timeouts, catalogs the bugs that cause double resumes and leaks, and shows how many stress-test iterations it takes to trust a fix.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift. Mutex requires iOS 18, macOS 15, or later.

Ownership, stated precisely

A continuation must be resumed exactly once. Restated as ownership:

  1. When withCheckedContinuation’s closure receives the continuation, the closure owns it.
  2. The closure may transfer ownership: to a completion handler it passes to an API, or into storage such as a property, a dictionary, or a queue.
  3. Whoever owns it must eventually consume it by calling resume, after which nobody owns it.
  4. Ownership must never be duplicated. Two parties that both believe they own the continuation will both resume it.

Most bugs are rule 4 violations hiding in plain sight. Capturing a continuation in two closures duplicates ownership. So does storing it in a property and capturing it in a cancellation handler. The fix is never “resume carefully”; it is to put the continuation where exactly one party can take it out.

A resolve-once slot

The primitive below holds the continuation and an optional early result under one lock. Any number of parties may call resolve; the first one wins and the rest are told they lost. It also handles the case where a resolver arrives before the continuation has been installed, which is what happens when a task is already cancelled on entry:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

/// Owns a continuation until exactly one resolver resumes it. Later resolvers are ignored.
final class ResolveOnce<Value: Sendable>: Sendable {
    private enum State {
        case awaitingContinuation
        case installed(CheckedContinuation<Value, any Error>)
        case resolvedEarly(Result<Value, any Error>)
        case finished
    }

    private let state = Mutex(State.awaitingContinuation)

    /// Installs the continuation. Returns false if a result already arrived, in which case
    /// the continuation has been resumed with it and the caller must not start any work.
    func install(_ continuation: CheckedContinuation<Value, any Error>) -> Bool {
        let early = state.withLock { state -> Result<Value, any Error>? in
            switch state {
            case .awaitingContinuation:
                state = .installed(continuation)
                return nil
            case .resolvedEarly(let result):
                state = .finished
                return result
            case .installed, .finished:
                preconditionFailure("install(_:) must be called exactly once")
            }
        }
        guard let early else { return true }
        continuation.resume(with: early)
        return false
    }

    /// Resolves with `result` if nobody has yet. Returns whether this call won.
    @discardableResult
    func resolve(_ result: Result<Value, any Error>) -> Bool {
        let winner = state.withLock { state -> CheckedContinuation<Value, any Error>?? in
            switch state {
            case .awaitingContinuation:
                state = .resolvedEarly(result)
                return .some(nil)                 // Won; the continuation will be resumed on install.
            case .installed(let continuation):
                state = .finished
                return .some(continuation)        // Won; resume now, outside the lock.
            case .resolvedEarly, .finished:
                return nil                        // Lost.
            }
        }
        guard let winner else { return false }
        winner?.resume(with: result)
        return true
    }
}

stateDiagram-v2
    accTitle: A resolve-once slot accepts exactly one result, whichever party arrives first
    [*] --> AwaitingContinuation
    AwaitingContinuation --> Installed: install(continuation)
    AwaitingContinuation --> ResolvedEarly: resolve(result), wins
    ResolvedEarly --> Finished: install resumes immediately, returns false
    Installed --> Finished: resolve(result), wins and resumes
    Finished --> Finished: later resolve calls lose

Every transition happens inside withLock, so the operation, the cancellation handler, and a timeout can call into it from different threads at the same instant and exactly one will win. The continuation is always resumed outside the lock, because resuming may run code that tries to take the same lock.

A legacy operation with an awkward cancellation contract

Real cancellable APIs disagree about what cancel() does. The fake below models the three contracts seen in practice:

enum CancelContract: Sendable {
    /// cancel() makes the operation call its completion with an error, synchronously.
    case completesWithError
    /// cancel() suppresses the completion entirely.
    case suppressesCompletion
    /// cancel() is best effort: the completion may still run later, with a success.
    case mayStillComplete
}

struct JobCancelled: Error {}

/// A cancellable callback-based job, standing in for an SDK.
final class LegacyJob: Sendable {
    private struct State {
        var completion: (@Sendable (Result<Int, any Error>) -> Void)?
        var cancelled = false
        var started = false
    }

    private let state = Mutex(State())
    let contract: CancelContract
    let duration: Duration

    init(contract: CancelContract, duration: Duration) {
        self.contract = contract
        self.duration = duration
    }

    var wasStarted: Bool {
        state.withLock { $0.started }
    }

    func start(completion: @escaping @Sendable (Result<Int, any Error>) -> Void) {
        state.withLock { state in
            state.completion = completion
            state.started = true
        }
        let nanoseconds = Int(duration.components.attoseconds / 1_000_000_000) + Int(duration.components.seconds) * 1_000_000_000
        DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + .nanoseconds(nanoseconds)) { [self] in
            let completion = state.withLock { state -> (@Sendable (Result<Int, any Error>) -> Void)? in
                if state.cancelled && contract != .mayStillComplete { return nil }
                defer { state.completion = nil }
                return state.completion
            }
            completion?(.success(42))
        }
    }

    func cancel() {
        let completion = state.withLock { state -> (@Sendable (Result<Int, any Error>) -> Void)? in
            state.cancelled = true
            guard contract == .completesWithError else { return nil }
            defer { state.completion = nil }
            return state.completion
        }
        completion?(.failure(JobCancelled()))
    }
}

Under .completesWithError, a naive wrapper that resumes from both the completion handler and the cancellation handler double-resumes. Under .suppressesCompletion, a wrapper that relies on the completion handler alone leaks. Under .mayStillComplete, either mistake can happen depending on timing. One wrapper built on ResolveOnce is correct under all three:

func run(_ job: LegacyJob) async throws -> Int {
    let slot = ResolveOnce<Int>()
    return try await withTaskCancellationHandler {
        try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
            guard slot.install(continuation) else { return }   // Already cancelled: do not start.
            job.start { result in
                slot.resolve(result)
            }
        }
    } onCancel: {
        slot.resolve(.failure(CancellationError()))            // Claim the result first...
        job.cancel()                                           // ...then tell the job to stop.
    }
}

The order inside onCancel matters. Resolving before calling job.cancel() guarantees that cancellation is reported as CancellationError, the error Swift code expects, even under the contract where cancel() synchronously calls the completion with the SDK’s own error. That call then loses the race and is ignored.

The guard slot.install(continuation) handles the timing the cancellation handlers article calls “case 1”: if the task was already cancelled, the handler ran first, resolved the slot, and install resumes the continuation immediately and returns false, so the job is never started.

func outcome(of job: LegacyJob, cancelAfter delay: Duration?) async -> String {
    let task = Task { try await run(job) }
    if let delay {
        try? await Task.sleep(for: delay)
        task.cancel()
    }
    switch await task.result {
    case .success(let value): return "value \(value)"
    case .failure(let error as CancellationError): _ = error; return "cancelled"
    case .failure(let error): return "failed: \(error)"
    }
}

for contract in [CancelContract.completesWithError, .suppressesCompletion, .mayStillComplete] {
    let completed = await outcome(of: LegacyJob(contract: contract, duration: .milliseconds(5)), cancelAfter: nil)
    let cancelled = await outcome(of: LegacyJob(contract: contract, duration: .seconds(5)), cancelAfter: .milliseconds(10))
    assert(completed == "value 42", "\(contract): completes normally")
    assert(cancelled == "cancelled", "\(contract): cancellation is reported as CancellationError")
}

let neverStarted = LegacyJob(contract: .suppressesCompletion, duration: .seconds(5))
let preCancelled = Task {
    withUnsafeCurrentTask { $0?.cancel() }
    return try await run(neverStarted)
}
let preCancelledValue = try? await preCancelled.value
assert(preCancelledValue == nil)
assert(!neverStarted.wasStarted, "A task cancelled on entry never starts the job")

Every contract completes normally when left alone and reports CancellationError when cancelled, within milliseconds rather than after the five-second job duration. For the .mayStillComplete contract, the job’s late success arrives five seconds later, finds the slot finished, and is discarded.

Timeouts are just another resolver

Because ResolveOnce accepts any number of resolvers, a timeout is one more party racing to resolve:

struct OperationTimedOut: Error {}

func run(_ job: LegacyJob, timeout: Duration) async throws -> Int {
    let slot = ResolveOnce<Int>()
    let timer = Task {
        try await Task.sleep(for: timeout)
        if slot.resolve(.failure(OperationTimedOut())) {
            job.cancel()
        }
    }
    defer { timer.cancel() }
    return try await withTaskCancellationHandler {
        try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
            guard slot.install(continuation) else { return }
            job.start { result in slot.resolve(result) }
        }
    } onCancel: {
        slot.resolve(.failure(CancellationError()))
        job.cancel()
    }
}

do {
    _ = try await run(LegacyJob(contract: .mayStillComplete, duration: .seconds(5)), timeout: .milliseconds(20))
    assertionFailure("A five-second job cannot beat a 20 ms timeout")
} catch is OperationTimedOut {
}
let quickResult = try await run(LegacyJob(contract: .mayStillComplete, duration: .milliseconds(5)), timeout: .seconds(1))
assert(quickResult == 42)

The timer only cancels the job if it won the race, which keeps it from cancelling a job that already succeeded. The defer cancels the timer task on every exit, so a fast success does not leave a sleeping timer behind.

Unlike the task-group timeout in the task groups article, this one returns as soon as the timer fires, even if the job ignores cancel(). The task group version must wait for its children; a continuation-based wrapper has no child to wait for. That makes it the right shape for legacy operations that cannot be interrupted, at the cost of the job possibly continuing in the background after the caller has moved on.

A catalog of double resumes and leaks

Almost every continuation bug in practice is one of these:

Bug Symptom Fix
Missing return after resuming on an error path Double resume Resume as the last statement, or return immediately after
Both success and failure callbacks fire Double resume Route both through a resolve-once slot
Completion races cancellation or timeout Intermittent double resume Make every resolver go through one slot
A newer request overwrites a stored continuation Leak of the older one Reject, join, or resume the older one before replacing it
cancel() suppresses the completion Leak on cancellation Resolve from the cancellation handler
Early guard ... else { return } inside the closure Leak Resume with an error in the else branch
Delegate held weakly and deallocated mid-operation Leak Retain the delegate for the operation’s lifetime
Continuation resumed while holding a lock Deadlock, not a crash Take the continuation out under the lock, resume after

The first row deserves an example, because it hides in code that looks finished:

func parse(_ data: Data?) async throws -> String {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyParse(data) { text, error in
            if let error {
                continuation.resume(throwing: error)
                // Missing return: execution falls through.
            }
            continuation.resume(returning: text ?? "")
        }
    }
}
// Fatal error: SWIFT TASK CONTINUATION MISUSE: parse(_:) tried to resume its continuation
// more than once, returning ...

Converting the (T?, Error?) callback pair into a Result first, then calling resume(with:) once, eliminates the whole class of bug.

How much stress testing is enough?

Races between completion, cancellation, and timeout happen only for particular interleavings. A test that runs once tells you little. If a bug manifests in a fraction \(p\) of runs, then the probability that \(N\) independent runs all miss it is \((1 - p)^N\). To catch it with confidence \(c\), you need

\[N \ge \frac{\ln(1 - c)}{\ln(1 - p)} \approx \frac{-\ln(1 - c)}{p} .\]

A race that shows up once in a thousand runs, \(p = 0.001\), needs about 4,600 runs to be caught with 99% confidence. A race at \(p = 0.01\) needs about 460. Concurrency tests should therefore loop, with randomized timing, and run in optimized builds as well as debug ones, since timing changes between them.

/// A deterministic generator, so a failing stress run can be replayed.
struct SplitMix64: RandomNumberGenerator {
    private var state: UInt64

    init(seed: UInt64) {
        state = seed
    }

    mutating func next() -> UInt64 {
        state &+= 0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15
        var z = state
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) &* 0xBF58_476D_1CE4_E5B9
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) &* 0x94D0_49BB_1331_11EB
        return z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

func stressCancellationRace(iterations: Int, seed: UInt64) async -> (completed: Int, cancelled: Int) {
    var generator = SplitMix64(seed: seed)
    var completed = 0
    var cancelled = 0
    let contracts: [CancelContract] = [.completesWithError, .suppressesCompletion, .mayStillComplete]
    for _ in 0..<iterations {
        let contract = contracts.randomElement(using: &generator)!
        let jobTime = Duration.microseconds(Int.random(in: 0...400, using: &generator))
        let cancelTime = Duration.microseconds(Int.random(in: 0...400, using: &generator))
        let task = Task { try await run(LegacyJob(contract: contract, duration: jobTime)) }
        try? await Task.sleep(for: cancelTime)
        task.cancel()
        switch await task.result {
        case .success: completed += 1
        case .failure: cancelled += 1
        }
    }
    return (completed, cancelled)
}

let stress = await stressCancellationRace(iterations: 1_000, seed: 2026)
assert(stress.completed + stress.cancelled == 1_000, "Every iteration finished exactly once, with no hang or trap")
assert(stress.completed > 0 && stress.cancelled > 0, "Both sides of the race were exercised")
print("stress: \(stress.completed) completed, \(stress.cancelled) cancelled")

The assertions are deliberately weak about which side wins, since that depends on timing. What they check is the invariant: every iteration ends, exactly once, as a success or an error. A double resume would trap; a leak would hang the loop. The seeded generator makes a failing run reproducible: rerun with the same seed to get the same sequence of contracts and delays, though not the same thread interleavings.

On the test machine, 1,000 iterations took about one second, with between 6% and 30% of them completing before the cancellation arrived, depending on the run. Running the same loop with a naive wrapper, one that stores the continuation for the cancellation handler and captures it in the completion handler, trapped at iteration 7 with “SWIFT TASK CONTINUATION MISUSE: runNaive(_:) tried to resume its continuation more than once, throwing CancellationError()!”. That is the behavior the formula predicts for a race with a high \(p\): a bug that a single test run would probably have missed, found in a fraction of a second.

Summary

  • Treat a continuation as a resource with exactly one owner. Duplicated ownership, such as two closures or a property plus a handler, is the root of double resumes.
  • Route every party that can finish an operation, completion, cancellation, timeout, through one resolve-once slot under a lock, and resume outside the lock.
  • Handle a result that arrives before the continuation is installed, so pre-cancelled tasks never start work.
  • In cancellation handlers, claim the result before calling the legacy cancel(), so callers always see CancellationError.
  • A continuation-based timeout returns promptly even when the legacy operation cannot be interrupted.
  • Convert (T?, Error?) callbacks to Result and resume once; it removes the missing-return bug class.
  • Stress-test races in loops: catching a bug with probability \(p\) per run at confidence \(c\) needs about \(-\ln(1 - c)/p\) runs.

Exercise

Extend the wrapper so that several callers can await the same LegacyJob: the first caller starts it, later callers join, and each caller can be cancelled independently. The job itself should be cancelled only when the last waiter leaves. Give each waiter its own ResolveOnce, keep the set of waiters in a Mutex, and write a stress test that randomly adds waiters, cancels some, and lets the job finish, checking that every waiter ends exactly once and that the job is cancelled if and only if every waiter was.

Further reading

  • SE-0300: Continuations for interfacing async tasks with synchronous code, section “Checked continuations.”
  • SE-0528: Continuation, which enforces single ownership in the type system on iOS 27 and macOS 27.
  • withTaskCancellationHandler(operation:onCancel:isolation:).

Previous: Bridging Callback APIs with Checked Continuations. Next: Rejecting Stale Results After Request Replacement.

Return to the Concurrency roadmap.
entry.summary: A continuation wrapper is easy to write when exactly one thing can finish the operation. It becomes hard as soon as two things can: a completion handler and a cancellation, a response and a timeout, a success callback and a failure callback that a buggy SDK sometimes calls both of. Each of those pairs is a race to resume the same continuation, and the loser either crashes the process with a double resume or, if the wrapper is defensive in the wrong way, leaves the task suspended forever. The way out is to treat a continuation as a resource with exactly one owner at any moment, and to make “who resumes” a single atomic decision. This article builds a small resolve-once primitive, uses it to make a cancellable legacy operation correct under three different cancellation contracts, adds timeouts, catalogs the bugs that cause double resumes and leaks, and shows how many stress-test iterations it takes to trust a fix.

entry.title: Bridging Callback APIs with Checked Continuations in Swift

link.title: Bridging Callback APIs with Checked Continuations in Swift

entry.content:
A continuation is the bridge between the callback world and the async world. Inside withCheckedContinuation, the current task suspends and hands you an object; whoever calls resume on that object, from any thread and at any later time, wakes the task up with a value or an error. With it, a twenty-year-old completion-handler API becomes an async function in a dozen lines.

The bridge has exactly one rule: resume every continuation exactly once. Resume it twice and the program traps. Never resume it and the waiting task is suspended forever, holding whatever it captured. This article builds wrappers for the common shapes of callback API, shows the diagnostics for each kind of misuse, compares the checked, unsafe, and new Swift 6.4 noncopyable continuations, and lists the cases where you do not need a continuation at all.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. Performance numbers come from an optimized build on an Apple M1 Ultra. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift. The noncopyable Continuation type requires iOS 27, macOS 27, or later; its example was compiled but not executed on the macOS 26 test machine.

The four functions

Function Continuation type Resumes with
withCheckedContinuation CheckedContinuation<T, Never> A value
withCheckedThrowingContinuation CheckedContinuation<T, any Error> A value or an error
withUnsafeContinuation UnsafeContinuation<T, Never> A value, without misuse checks
withUnsafeThrowingContinuation UnsafeContinuation<T, any Error> A value or an error, without checks

All four run their closure immediately and synchronously, in the caller’s isolation, before the task suspends (SE-0300). That is what makes them safe to use for registration: the closure starts the legacy operation and stores or captures the continuation, then returns, and only then does the task suspend.

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A task suspends inside withCheckedContinuation until a callback resumes it
    participant T as Async caller
    participant W as withCheckedContinuation body
    participant L as Legacy API
    participant Q as Callback queue
    T->>W: call, body runs synchronously
    W->>L: start operation, pass a completion that captures the continuation
    W-->>T: body returns, task suspends and frees its thread
    L->>Q: operation completes later
    Q->>Q: completion calls continuation.resume(returning:)
    Q-->>T: task becomes runnable
    T->>T: continues on its own executor with the value

The continuation is Sendable, so completion handlers on any queue may resume it. After resume, the task continues on its own executor, so a main-actor caller is back on the main actor, whatever thread the callback used.

Shape 1: a single Result completion

The simplest and most common shape is a function that calls one completion handler exactly once, with either a value or an error:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

struct Place: Equatable, Sendable {
    let name: String
}

enum GeocodeError: Error, Equatable {
    case notFound(String)
}

/// A legacy API: calls `completion` exactly once, on a background queue.
func legacyGeocode(_ query: String, completion: @escaping @Sendable (Result<Place, GeocodeError>) -> Void) {
    DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + .milliseconds(5)) {
        completion(query.isEmpty ? .failure(.notFound(query)) : .success(Place(name: query.capitalized)))
    }
}

func geocode(_ query: String) async throws -> Place {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyGeocode(query) { result in
            continuation.resume(with: result)
        }
    }
}

let place = try await geocode("lisbon")
assert(place == Place(name: "Lisbon"))
do {
    _ = try await geocode("")
    assertionFailure("An empty query must fail")
} catch GeocodeError.notFound(let query) {
    assert(query.isEmpty)
}

resume(with:) forwards a Result directly. The error arrives as any Error, because CheckedContinuation’s throwing form is untyped; the catch pattern recovers the concrete type.

This wrapper is correct only because the legacy function’s contract says it calls completion exactly once. That is the property to verify, from documentation or from the source, before writing any continuation wrapper. The rest of this article is about APIs that do not make that promise cleanly.

Shape 2: separate success and failure callbacks

Some APIs take two closures and promise, usually only in documentation, that exactly one of them runs:

/// Calls exactly one of `onSuccess` or `onFailure`, once.
func legacyFetchAvatar(
    userID: Int,
    onSuccess: @escaping @Sendable (Data) -> Void,
    onFailure: @escaping @Sendable (any Error) -> Void
) {
    DispatchQueue.global().async {
        if userID > 0 {
            onSuccess(Data(repeating: 0xAB, count: userID))
        } else {
            onFailure(URLError(.badURL))
        }
    }
}

func avatar(userID: Int) async throws -> Data {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyFetchAvatar(userID: userID) { data in
            continuation.resume(returning: data)
        } onFailure: { error in
            continuation.resume(throwing: error)
        }
    }
}

let avatarData = try await avatar(userID: 4)
assert(avatarData.count == 4)

The continuation is captured by two closures, so the compiler cannot prove only one of them calls it. A checked continuation catches a violation at run time. If you do not trust the “exactly one” promise, for example because a third-party SDK has been seen calling both on some error path, add a guard that makes extra calls harmless:

/// Wraps a continuation so that only the first resume takes effect. Later ones are ignored.
final class ResumeOnce<T: Sendable>: Sendable {
    private let continuation: Mutex<CheckedContinuation<T, any Error>?>

    init(_ continuation: CheckedContinuation<T, any Error>) {
        self.continuation = Mutex(continuation)
    }

    func resume(with result: Result<T, any Error>) {
        let pending = continuation.withLock { stored in
            defer { stored = nil }
            return stored
        }
        pending?.resume(with: result)
    }
}

Use it deliberately. It turns a crash into silently discarded callbacks, which is the right trade only when the extra calls are known to be benign duplicates.

Shape 3: callbacks that may run synchronously

Many APIs call their completion handler synchronously in some cases, such as a cache hit or an invalid argument, and asynchronously otherwise. Continuations handle both, because resuming before the task suspends is allowed: the task simply does not suspend.

final class LegacyThumbnailCache: Sendable {
    private let cached = Mutex<[String: Int]>(["logo": 128])

    /// Calls `completion` synchronously for a cache hit, asynchronously for a miss.
    func thumbnail(named name: String, completion: @escaping @Sendable (Int) -> Void) {
        if let size = cached.withLock({ $0[name] }) {
            completion(size)
            return
        }
        DispatchQueue.global().async { [self] in
            cached.withLock { $0[name] = 64 }
            completion(64)
        }
    }
}

func thumbnailSize(_ name: String, from cache: LegacyThumbnailCache) async -> Int {
    await withCheckedContinuation { continuation in
        cache.thumbnail(named: name) { size in
            continuation.resume(returning: size)
        }
    }
}

let thumbnailCache = LegacyThumbnailCache()
let hit = await thumbnailSize("logo", from: thumbnailCache)
let miss = await thumbnailSize("banner", from: thumbnailCache)
assert(hit == 128 && miss == 64)

This is one of the advantages of continuations over the old habit of “always dispatch the completion asynchronously to be safe”: the wrapper does not care which path the API takes.

Shape 4: a delegate that answers one request

Some single-shot operations report through a delegate: a permission prompt, a document picker, an authentication session. The continuation must be stored until the delegate method fires, and the storage must handle a second request arriving while the first is pending:

enum PermissionError: Error, Equatable {
    case requestAlreadyPending
}

/// A delegate-style API: `onDecision` is called once per request, later.
final class LegacyPermissionPrompt: Sendable {
    let onDecision = Mutex<(@Sendable (Bool) -> Void)?>(nil)

    func present(userWillGrant: Bool) {
        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + .milliseconds(10)) { [self] in
            onDecision.withLock { $0 }?(userWillGrant)
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
final class PermissionRequester {
    private let prompt = LegacyPermissionPrompt()
    private var pending: CheckedContinuation<Bool, any Error>?

    init() {
        prompt.onDecision.withLock {
            $0 = { [weak self] granted in
                Task { @MainActor in self?.complete(granted) }
            }
        }
    }

    func requestAccess(userWillGrant: Bool) async throws -> Bool {
        guard pending == nil else { throw PermissionError.requestAlreadyPending }
        return try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
            pending = continuation
            prompt.present(userWillGrant: userWillGrant)
        }
    }

    private func complete(_ granted: Bool) {
        let continuation = pending
        pending = nil
        continuation?.resume(returning: granted)
    }
}

let requester = PermissionRequester()
async let firstRequest = requester.requestAccess(userWillGrant: true)
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(2))
do {
    _ = try await requester.requestAccess(userWillGrant: false)
    assertionFailure("A second request while one is pending must be rejected")
} catch PermissionError.requestAlreadyPending {
}
let granted = try await firstRequest
assert(granted)

Three details carry the correctness:

  • The check and the store happen in one synchronous stretch. requestAccess runs on the main actor, and withCheckedThrowingContinuation runs its closure synchronously, so no other call can slip in between guard pending == nil and pending = continuation.
  • The continuation leaves storage before it is resumed. complete clears pending first, so a duplicate delegate call finds nothing to resume.
  • Concurrent requests have a policy. Here the second one is rejected. Joining it to the first, by storing an array of continuations and resuming all of them, is equally valid; silently overwriting the first continuation is not, because that leaks it.

What misuse looks like

The “checked” in CheckedContinuation means the runtime tracks each continuation and reports both kinds of misuse. On the test toolchain:

func resumesTwice() async -> Int {
    await withCheckedContinuation { continuation in
        continuation.resume(returning: 1)
        continuation.resume(returning: 2)
    }
}
// Fatal error: SWIFT TASK CONTINUATION MISUSE: resumesTwice() tried to resume its
// continuation more than once, returning 2!

func neverResumes() async -> Int {
    await withCheckedContinuation { (continuation: CheckedContinuation<Int, Never>) in
        // Forgot to start the operation, or the operation's error path never calls back.
    }
}
// SWIFT TASK CONTINUATION MISUSE: neverResumes() leaked its continuation without resuming it.
// This may cause tasks waiting on it to remain suspended forever.

A double resume is a fatal error: the program stops at the second resume, with the function name in the message. A leak is reported as a printed warning when the continuation object is destroyed without having been resumed; the waiting task stays suspended, and nothing else happens. If the continuation is still referenced somewhere, for example stored in a property that is never cleared, no warning appears at all, and the task simply hangs. Tests that exercise error paths, such as timeouts, invalid input, and cancellation, are the best defense against leaks.

The function name in both messages comes from a function: String = #function parameter on withCheckedContinuation, so it names the function that created the continuation. That makes the wrapper function easy to find in a crash report.

Checked or unsafe?

UnsafeContinuation has the same API without the bookkeeping. It is faster, and it turns misuse into undefined behavior. A microbenchmark that creates a continuation and resumes it immediately, 200,000 times in an optimized build, measured:

Continuation Time per create-and-resume
CheckedContinuation about 340 ns
UnsafeContinuation about 180 ns

The difference, about 160 ns, matters only when bridging happens hundreds of thousands of times per second: per-packet or per-sample callbacks in a hot loop. For a network request, a file read, or a permission prompt, it is unmeasurable next to the operation itself. Use checked continuations by default. If profiling shows the checks matter, switch to unsafe only after the wrapper has been exercised thoroughly with checked continuations, and keep tests that run its error paths.

Swift 6.4: a continuation the compiler checks

Swift 6.4 adds a third option, Continuation<Success, Failure> (SE-0528), obtained with withContinuation(of:throwing:_:). It is noncopyable, and each resume method consumes it. Resuming twice is therefore a compile-time error, and a continuation that is dropped without being resumed traps immediately instead of leaking silently. It has no run-time bookkeeping on the success path, so it costs about what an unsafe continuation does. It also adopts typed throws: throwing: NetworkError.self gives a continuation, and a call site, that can throw only NetworkError.

// Does not compile in Swift 6 mode.
@available(iOS 27, macOS 27, *)
func resumesTwiceNoncopyable() async -> Int {
    await withContinuation(of: Int.self) { continuation in
        continuation.resume(returning: 1)
        continuation.resume(returning: 2)
    }
}
// error: 'continuation' consumed more than once

The same ownership rules that prevent the double resume also prevent the most common bridging pattern. A noncopyable value cannot be captured by an escaping closure, and completion handlers are escaping:

// Does not compile in Swift 6 mode.
@available(iOS 27, macOS 27, *)
func geocodeNoncopyable(_ query: String) async throws -> Place {
    try await withContinuation(of: Place.self, throwing: (any Error).self) { continuation in
        legacyGeocode(query) { result in
            continuation.resume(with: result.mapError { $0 })
        }
    }
}
// error: noncopyable 'continuation' cannot be consumed when captured by an escaping closure
// or borrowed by a non-Escapable type

So the new type does not replace CheckedContinuation for completion handlers. The proposal provides CheckedContinuation(continuation) to convert when a continuation must flow into callbacks. Where Continuation shines is code that stores continuations and resumes them later from a single place: actor-based waiters, queues of pending requests, permit pools, and gates like the ones in the reentrancy and cancellation handler articles. There, moving the continuation out of storage and consuming it with resume is exactly the discipline those designs already follow by hand, and the compiler now enforces it.

@available(iOS 27, macOS 27, *)
actor OneShotSignal {
    private var waiter: Continuation<Int, Never>?
    private var value: Int?

    func wait() async -> Int {
        if let value { return value }
        return await withContinuation(of: Int.self) { continuation in
            waiter = consume continuation
        }
    }

    func fire(_ newValue: Int) {
        value = newValue
        if let waiter = waiter.take() {
            waiter.resume(returning: newValue)   // Consumed: cannot be resumed again.
        }
    }
}

if #available(iOS 27, macOS 27, *) {
    let signal = OneShotSignal()
    async let waited = signal.wait()
    try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(5))
    await signal.fire(42)
    let signalled = await waited
    assert(signalled == 42)
}

Optional.take() moves the stored continuation out and leaves nil behind, so storage and resumption cannot get out of step. Overwriting a stored continuation without resuming it would destroy it, which traps, turning the silent hang of a leaked CheckedContinuation into a crash at the line that caused it.

When you do not need a continuation

Before writing a wrapper, check whether one already exists:

  • Objective-C completion handlers are imported as async automatically (SE-0297). A method like - (void)fetchWithCompletion:(void (^)(NSData *, NSError *))completion is also available as func fetch() async throws -> Data. Most Apple frameworks already provide these.
  • Foundation has async APIs for most I/O: URLSession.data(for:), FileHandle.bytes, URL.lines, NotificationCenter.notifications(named:).
  • Multi-shot callbacks want a stream, not a continuation. A continuation resumes once. A callback that fires repeatedly, such as progress updates, location fixes, or ticks, belongs in an AsyncStream, as the AsyncStream article shows.

Summary

  • withChecked(Throwing)Continuation runs its closure synchronously, then suspends until resume is called, from any thread.
  • Resume exactly once. A double resume is a fatal error naming the function; a leak prints a warning when the continuation is destroyed, or hangs silently if it is still stored.
  • Verify the “called exactly once” contract of every API you wrap. Guard two-callback APIs, store delegate continuations with a policy for concurrent requests, and clear storage before resuming.
  • Checked continuations cost about 340 ns per use against 180 ns for unsafe ones; use checked by default.
  • Swift 6.4’s noncopyable Continuation turns double resumes into compile errors and leaks into traps, but cannot be captured by escaping completion handlers. Use it for stored waiters on iOS 27 and macOS 27.
  • Prefer existing async APIs, including automatically imported Objective-C ones, and use streams for multi-shot callbacks.

Exercise

Wrap a legacy Downloader whose start(url:completion:) calls completion exactly once, but whose cancel() method, if called while a download is in progress, calls completion with a cancellation error, and if called after completion, does nothing. Write func download(_ url: URL) async throws -> Data using a checked continuation, then add cancellation support with withTaskCancellationHandler. Write tests for completion, failure, cancellation before start, cancellation mid-download, and cancellation after completion, and verify that no test produces a continuation misuse message. The next article covers the patterns these tests will need.

Further reading

  • SE-0300: Continuations for interfacing async tasks with synchronous code.
  • SE-0528: Continuation, safe and performant async continuations.
  • SE-0297: Concurrency Interoperability with Objective-C.
  • Swift concurrency: Update a sample app, WWDC21, on migrating completion handlers.

entry.summary: A continuation is the bridge between the callback world and the async world. Inside withCheckedContinuation, the current task suspends and hands you an object; whoever calls resume on that object, from any thread and at any later time, wakes the task up with a value or an error. With it, a twenty-year-old completion-handler API becomes an async function in a dozen lines. The bridge has exactly one rule: resume every continuation exactly once. Resume it twice and the program traps. Never resume it and the waiting task is suspended forever, holding whatever it captured. This article builds wrappers for the common shapes of callback API, shows the diagnostics for each kind of misuse, compares the checked, unsafe, and new Swift 6.4 noncopyable continuations, and lists the cases where you do not need a continuation at all.

entry.title: Buffering, Backpressure, and Stream Termination in Swift

link.title: Buffering, Backpressure, and Stream Termination in Swift

entry.content:
Whenever a producer can generate values faster than a consumer can handle them, something has to give. The values can pile up in a buffer, which costs memory and makes the consumer see increasingly stale data. Some values can be dropped. Or the producer can be made to wait, which is backpressure: the consumer’s pace propagates back to the source.

AsyncStream chooses buffering and dropping. Its yield never waits, so it cannot apply backpressure; it can only decide what to do with values that arrive while the consumer is busy. This article quantifies that choice, measures each buffering policy, builds a small bounded channel that does apply backpressure, and pins down exactly what happens to buffered values when a stream finishes, fails, or is cancelled.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift.

A buffer is a queue, and queues have arithmetic

Suppose a producer emits values at rate \(\lambda\) and a consumer processes them at rate \(\mu\). If \(\lambda \le \mu\), any buffer stays small: it absorbs bursts and drains between them. If \(\lambda > \mu\) for a sustained period of length \(t\), the excess accumulates:

\[Q(t) = (\lambda - \mu)\, t .\]

A sensor producing 1,000 readings per second, consumed by UI code that handles 60 per second, accumulates 940 readings per second. After a minute, an unbounded buffer holds 56,400 readings, and the consumer is a minute behind reality.

Staleness follows from Little’s law: a value that enters a buffer holding \(L\) values, drained at rate \(\mu\), waits about

\[W = \frac{L}{\mu}\]

before it is handled. With a 100-value buffer drained at 60 per second, the consumer is always about 1.7 seconds behind. For UI state, that is useless: the user sees where they were. For an audit log, it may be fine, as long as memory allows. The policy has to match what the values mean.

The three buffering policies

AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream take a bufferingPolicy when created:

Policy When the buffer is full Keeps Typical use
.unbounded (default) Never full Everything Bounded, bursty sources where every value matters
.bufferingOldest(n) Drops the new value The first n values First-come work where later duplicates are redundant
.bufferingNewest(n) Drops the oldest buffered value The latest n values State, progress, positions: anything where newer supersedes older

yield reports what happened to each value through YieldResult: .enqueued(remaining:), .dropped(element), or .terminated. The experiment below yields 1,000 values while the consumer is busy elsewhere, then lets the consumer drain whatever the stream kept:

import Synchronization

struct StreamRun: Sendable {
    let delivered: [Int]
    let enqueued: Int
    let dropped: Int
}

func flood(policy: AsyncStream<Int>.Continuation.BufferingPolicy) async -> StreamRun {
    let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self, bufferingPolicy: policy)
    var enqueued = 0
    var dropped = 0
    for value in 0..<1_000 {          // The consumer is not reading yet: everything goes to the buffer.
        switch continuation.yield(value) {
        case .enqueued: enqueued += 1
        case .dropped: dropped += 1
        case .terminated: break
        @unknown default: break
        }
    }
    continuation.finish()
    var delivered: [Int] = []
    for await value in stream {
        delivered.append(value)
    }
    return StreamRun(delivered: delivered, enqueued: enqueued, dropped: dropped)
}

let unbounded = await flood(policy: .unbounded)
assert(unbounded.delivered == Array(0..<1_000) && unbounded.dropped == 0)

let oldest = await flood(policy: .bufferingOldest(10))
assert(oldest.delivered == Array(0..<10) && oldest.dropped == 990, "Kept the first ten, dropped every later value")

let newest = await flood(policy: .bufferingNewest(10))
assert(newest.delivered == Array(990..<1_000) && newest.dropped == 990, "Kept the latest ten, evicting older ones")

The unbounded stream held all 1,000 values. Each bounded policy kept exactly ten and dropped 990, but different ones: bufferingOldest kept 0 through 9 and refused everything after; bufferingNewest kept 990 through 999, evicting older values as newer ones arrived. When a consumer is already waiting at the moment of a yield, the value is handed to it directly without touching the buffer, so in a live stream a bounded policy can deliver one more value than its limit.

Two details matter in practice:

  • .unbounded is the default. A stream created without a policy has no memory limit. That is fine for a delegate that reports a handful of events. It is a slow leak for a high-frequency source, such as motion data, audio levels, or download progress, paired with a consumer that occasionally stalls.
  • bufferingNewest(1) is “latest value” semantics. The consumer always sees the most recent state, never more than one value behind. For UI it is usually the right policy; staleness is bounded by one consumer iteration.

AsyncStream cannot apply backpressure

Dropping values is acceptable when values supersede each other. It is not acceptable for a file upload, a database import, or a log shipper, where every value must be processed. For those, the producer must slow down when the consumer cannot keep up.

AsyncStream.Continuation.yield is synchronous. It cannot suspend the producer, so it cannot transmit the consumer’s pace. A proposal to add backpressure to AsyncStream, SE-0406, was returned for revision and is not part of the Swift 6.4 standard library. Until something like it ships, backpressure needs one of three designs:

  1. Pull-based production. If the source can produce on request, use AsyncStream(unfolding:) or a custom AsyncSequence. The producer runs only when the consumer calls next(), so it can never get ahead.
  2. A channel whose send suspends. The swift-async-algorithms package provides AsyncChannel, where send suspends until a consumer takes the value. A bounded buffer generalizes that to “suspend only when n values are waiting.”
  3. Source-level flow control. Pause and resume the underlying source, for example by suspending a URLSessionTask or stopping a sensor, driven by buffer depth. This is the only option when the source itself cannot wait, such as a network socket that keeps receiving.

A bounded channel with backpressure

A bounded channel is a buffer of capacity \(n\) where send suspends while the buffer is full and receive suspends while it is empty. An actor makes the bookkeeping straightforward:

/// A single-consumer channel whose `send` suspends while `capacity` values are waiting.
actor BoundedChannel<Element: Sendable> {
    private var buffer: [Element] = []
    private let capacity: Int
    private var waitingSenders: [CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>] = []
    private var waitingReceiver: CheckedContinuation<Element?, Never>?
    private var isFinished = false
    private(set) var peakBuffered = 0

    init(capacity: Int) {
        precondition(capacity > 0)
        self.capacity = capacity
    }

    /// Returns false if the channel was finished before the value could be sent.
    func send(_ element: Element) async -> Bool {
        while buffer.count >= capacity && !isFinished {
            await withCheckedContinuation { waitingSenders.append($0) }
        }
        guard !isFinished else { return false }
        if let receiver = waitingReceiver {
            waitingReceiver = nil
            receiver.resume(returning: element)
        } else {
            buffer.append(element)
            peakBuffered = max(peakBuffered, buffer.count)
        }
        return true
    }

    /// Returns nil once the channel is finished and drained.
    func receive() async -> Element? {
        if !buffer.isEmpty {
            let element = buffer.removeFirst()
            if !waitingSenders.isEmpty {
                waitingSenders.removeFirst().resume()
            }
            return element
        }
        if isFinished { return nil }
        return await withCheckedContinuation { waitingReceiver = $0 }
    }

    func finish() {
        isFinished = true
        waitingReceiver?.resume(returning: nil)
        waitingReceiver = nil
        for sender in waitingSenders {
            sender.resume()
        }
        waitingSenders.removeAll()
    }
}

Two parts of this design come straight from the actor reentrancy article. The while loop in send, rather than an if, re-checks the condition after every wake-up, because another sender may have filled the freed slot while this one was suspended. And every continuation is removed from the actor’s state at the moment it is resumed, so none can be resumed twice.

With a fast producer and a slow consumer, the buffer never exceeds its capacity and nothing is lost:

let channel = BoundedChannel<Int>(capacity: 8)
let channelProducer = Task { () -> Int in
    var sent = 0
    for value in 0..<200 {
        if await channel.send(value) { sent += 1 }
    }
    await channel.finish()
    return sent
}

var channelDelivered: [Int] = []
while let value = await channel.receive() {
    channelDelivered.append(value)
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .microseconds(200))     // A slow consumer.
}
let channelSent = await channelProducer.value
let channelPeak = await channel.peakBuffered
assert(channelSent == 200 && channelDelivered == Array(0..<200), "Every value, in order")
assert(channelPeak <= 8, "Memory is bounded by the capacity")

The producer ran exactly as fast as the consumer allowed: whenever eight values were waiting, its send suspended until the consumer took one. Memory is bounded by the capacity, and staleness by \(W = n/\mu\).

This channel is deliberately small, and a production version needs more:

  • Cancellation. A sender cancelled while suspended stays suspended until space appears. Removing it requires the cancellation-handler pattern from the cancellation handlers article, with an identifier per waiter.
  • Multiple consumers. waitingReceiver holds a single continuation. More consumers need a queue of them.
  • Priority. Waiting senders are suspended through continuations, which hide the dependency from priority escalation, as the priority article shows.

For most code, a well-tested library type such as AsyncChannel is the better choice. Building one once is the best way to understand what it does.

Backpressure must hold at every stage

In a multi-stage pipeline, backpressure propagates only if every stage is pull-based or suspending. A single push-based stage breaks the chain:

flowchart LR
    accTitle: One push-based stage breaks backpressure propagation in a pipeline
    subgraph Good["Backpressure propagates"]
        A1["Source, pull-based"] --> B1["Transform, pulls from source"] --> C1["Bounded channel"] --> D1["Slow consumer"]
    end
    subgraph Broken["Backpressure stops at the AsyncStream"]
        A2["Source"] --> B2["Task that yields into AsyncStream"] --> C2[["Unbounded buffer grows"]] --> D2["Slow consumer"]
    end

The broken shape is common: a task reads from a pull-based source as fast as it can and yields every element into an AsyncStream for “decoupling.” The source is now read at full speed, the stream’s default buffer is unbounded, and the slow consumer’s pace never reaches the source. Either replace the stream with a suspending channel, or let the consumer pull from the source directly.

Termination and what happens to buffered values

A stream ends in one of three ways, and each treats the buffer differently:

let terminationLog = Mutex<[String]>([])

// 1. finish(): buffered values are delivered, then the loop ends normally.
let (finishing, finishingContinuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
finishingContinuation.onTermination = { reason in
    terminationLog.withLock { $0.append("finishing: \(reason)") }
}
for value in 1...3 { finishingContinuation.yield(value) }
finishingContinuation.finish()
var drained: [Int] = []
for await value in finishing { drained.append(value) }
assert(drained == [1, 2, 3])

// 2. finish(throwing:): buffered values are delivered, then the error is thrown.
struct FeedBroke: Error {}
let (failing, failingContinuation) = AsyncThrowingStream.makeStream(of: Int.self, throwing: (any Error).self)
for value in 1...3 { failingContinuation.yield(value) }
failingContinuation.finish(throwing: FeedBroke())
var beforeFailure: [Int] = []
do {
    for try await value in failing { beforeFailure.append(value) }
    assertionFailure("The stream must end with its error")
} catch is FeedBroke {
}
assert(beforeFailure == [1, 2, 3], "Values buffered before the error still arrive first")

// 3. Consumer cancellation while the consumer is busy in its loop body.
let (abandoned, abandonedContinuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
abandonedContinuation.onTermination = { reason in
    terminationLog.withLock { $0.append("abandoned: \(reason)") }
}
let abandoningConsumer = Task { () -> [String] in
    var seen: [String] = []
    for await value in abandoned {
        seen.append("\(value), cancelled: \(Task.isCancelled)")
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(50))         // Busy, not waiting in next().
    }
    return seen
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(5))
for value in 1...3 { abandonedContinuation.yield(value) }
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(10))
abandoningConsumer.cancel()
let yieldRightAfterCancel = abandonedContinuation.yield(4)
let seenAfterCancellation = await abandoningConsumer.value
if case .enqueued = yieldRightAfterCancel {} else {
    assertionFailure("The stream had not yet noticed the cancellation")
}
assert(seenAfterCancellation == ["1, cancelled: false", "2, cancelled: true", "3, cancelled: true", "4, cancelled: true"])
if case .terminated = abandonedContinuation.yield(5) {} else {
    assertionFailure("Once the consumer returned to next(), the stream terminated")
}
assert(terminationLog.withLock { $0 } == ["finishing: finished", "abandoned: cancelled"])

The third case surprised me when I first ran it, and it is worth reading the trace closely. The consumer was cancelled while it was busy in its loop body, sleeping, rather than waiting in next(). At that moment the stream did not know about the cancellation at all: a yield immediately after cancel() returned .enqueued. Only when the consumer came back and called next() did the stream terminate, run onTermination with .cancelled, and refuse further values. Even then, everything already in the buffer, including the value yielded after cancel(), was delivered to the cancelled loop before it ended.

When the consumer is instead waiting inside next() at the moment of cancellation, the stream terminates immediately: in a separate run, onTermination fired before cancel() even returned, and the next yield returned .terminated.

The consequences for design:

  • Finishing is graceful. A producer that calls finish() can rely on the consumer seeing everything already yielded. Use it for orderly shutdown.
  • Errors are ordered. finish(throwing:) does not jump the queue. A consumer that must react to the error immediately, for example to show “connection lost” without first rendering stale buffered updates, needs bufferingNewest(1) or a separate signal.
  • Cancellation is noticed at next(), and buffered values still drain. A cancelled consumer keeps receiving whatever is buffered, and the producer can keep yielding until the consumer next asks for a value. A consumer that must stop immediately should check Task.isCancelled at the top of its loop body and break; a producer that must stop immediately should not rely on yield returning .terminated promptly. Values that must not be lost, such as pending uploads, need the producer’s own record of what was delivered.

Choosing a design

Values are… Consumer may fall behind because… Use
State or progress, newer supersedes older UI updates are slower than the source bufferingNewest(1)
Events, occasional bursts, all needed Short stalls .unbounded, with a bounded source
Events, sustained high rate, all needed The consumer is fundamentally slower A suspending channel, or pull-based production
Work items, first submission wins Duplicates arrive while busy bufferingOldest(n)
Bytes from a network socket Disk or decoding is slower than the network Source-level flow control

Summary

  • When producers outpace consumers, buffers grow as \((\lambda - \mu)\,t\) and staleness as \(L / \mu\).
  • AsyncStream buffers or drops; its yield never suspends, so it cannot apply backpressure. The default policy is unbounded.
  • bufferingNewest(n) keeps the latest values and bufferingOldest(n) the first; with \(n = 10\), each kept ten of 1,000 and dropped 990.
  • For backpressure, use pull-based production or a channel whose send suspends. A bounded channel kept the buffer at its capacity of 8 while delivering all 200 values in order.
  • Backpressure holds only if every pipeline stage respects it.
  • finish() and finish(throwing:) deliver buffered values first. A stream notices consumer cancellation only at next(), and still delivers buffered values to the cancelled loop.

Exercise

Add cancellation support to BoundedChannel.send: a sender cancelled while waiting for space must return false promptly and leave no continuation behind, even if cancellation races with a receiver freeing a slot. Use withTaskCancellationHandler and give each waiting sender an identifier. Then build a three-stage pipeline, reading lines, parsing them, and writing records, connected by two bounded channels, and verify with peakBuffered that a slow writer keeps both channels at their capacity rather than letting the reader run ahead.

Further reading

  • SE-0314: AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream, on buffering policies.
  • SE-0406: Backpressure support for AsyncStream, returned for revision.
  • swift-async-algorithms, including AsyncChannel and AsyncThrowingChannel.
  • Parallel Algorithms and MapReduce in Swift, for the work-and-span view of pipeline throughput.

Previous: Building Streams with AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream. Next: Bridging Callback APIs with Checked Continuations.
