entry.title: Building Streams with AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream in Swift

link.title: Building Streams with AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream in Swift

entry.content:
Most event sources in an app were built before Swift concurrency: delegates that report location fixes, callbacks that fire for every download chunk, observers that receive notifications, timers that tick. AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream adapt them to AsyncSequence, so consumers can write for await event in events and get cancellation, structured lifetimes, and sequential processing for free.

The adapter has two halves: a continuation that the producer pushes values into, and a stream that one consumer iterates. Getting the boundary right means deciding who finishes the stream, what happens when the consumer goes away, and what to do when there is more than one consumer. This article builds adapters for a callback API and a delegate API, shows the lifecycle rules with tests, and fixes the single-consumer limitation with a broadcaster.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift. Mutex requires iOS 18, macOS 15, or later.

The two halves

AsyncStream.makeStream(of:bufferingPolicy:) (SE-0388) returns both halves at once:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

let (numbers, numbersContinuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)

let producer = Task {
    for value in 1...5 {
        numbersContinuation.yield(value)
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(2))
    }
    numbersContinuation.finish()
}

var received: [Int] = []
for await value in numbers {
    received.append(value)
}
await producer.value
assert(received == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

flowchart LR
    accTitle: A producer yields into a continuation, the stream buffers, and one consumer pulls
    P["Producer: callbacks, delegate, or task"] -- "yield(value)" --> C["Continuation, Sendable"]
    P -- "finish()" --> C
    C --> B[["Buffer, governed by bufferingPolicy"]]
    B --> I["Stream iterator"]
    I -- "for await" --> K["Single consumer"]
    K -. "consumer task cancelled, or stream released" .-> T["onTermination(.cancelled)"]
    C -. "finish()" .-> T2["onTermination(.finished)"]
    T --> P
    T2 --> P

The continuation is Sendable, so callbacks on any thread can call yield without further synchronization. yield never suspends: it hands the value to a waiting consumer or appends it to the stream’s buffer and returns immediately. That makes AsyncStream a push source, unlike the pull-based sequences of the previous article. The buffer is the stream’s only defense against a producer that outpaces its consumer, and the backpressure article is about choosing its policy.

There is also an older, closure-based initializer, AsyncStream { continuation in ... }, which runs the closure immediately with the continuation. It is convenient when all setup fits in one place; makeStream is clearer when the continuation must be stored in an object that outlives the setup code.

Adapting a callback API

Here is a legacy ticker of the kind found in media players and sensor SDKs: you start it with a handler, it calls the handler repeatedly on a background queue, and you must stop it explicitly.

/// A callback-based API: calls `handler` every `interval` until stopped.
final class LegacyTicker: Sendable {
    private struct State {
        var timer: DispatchSourceTimer?
        var ticks = 0
    }

    private let state = Mutex(State())
    private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "legacy.ticker")

    func start(interval: DispatchTimeInterval, handler: @escaping @Sendable (Int) -> Void) {
        let timer = DispatchSource.makeTimerSource(queue: queue)
        timer.schedule(deadline: .now() + interval, repeating: interval)
        timer.setEventHandler { [self] in
            let tick = state.withLock { state -> Int in
                state.ticks += 1
                return state.ticks
            }
            handler(tick)
        }
        state.withLock { $0.timer = timer }
        timer.resume()
    }

    func stop() {
        state.withLock { state in
            state.timer?.cancel()
            state.timer = nil
        }
    }

    var isRunning: Bool {
        state.withLock { $0.timer != nil }
    }
}

The adapter wires the handler to yield and wires stream termination to stop():

extension LegacyTicker {
    func ticks(every interval: DispatchTimeInterval) -> AsyncStream<Int> {
        let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
        continuation.onTermination = { [self] _ in
            stop()       // The consumer cancelled or the stream finished: stop producing.
        }
        start(interval: interval) { tick in
            continuation.yield(tick)
        }
        return stream
    }
}

func firstTicks(from ticker: LegacyTicker, count: Int) async -> [Int] {
    var ticks: [Int] = []
    for await tick in ticker.ticks(every: .milliseconds(5)) {
        ticks.append(tick)
        if ticks.count == count { break }
    }
    return ticks
}

let ticker = LegacyTicker()
let threeTicks = await firstTicks(from: ticker, count: 3)
assert(threeTicks == [1, 2, 3])
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(10))
assert(!ticker.isRunning, "The stream was released, which terminated it and stopped the ticker")

When firstTicks returned, the stream it created went out of scope. The stream terminated with .cancelled, onTermination ran, and the legacy timer stopped. The consumer never had to know the ticker existed. That chain, consumer leaves, stream terminates, producer stops, is the most important thing an adapter does. Without onTermination, the ticker would keep firing into a stream nobody reads, forever.

Notice what triggered the termination: not the break, but the stream being released. The next section shows why that distinction matters.

Adapting a delegate API

Delegate-based APIs need one more piece: an object to be the delegate, which forwards each delegate call to the continuation. That object must stay alive for as long as the stream, so the stream’s termination handler is a natural place to retain it:

struct Fix: Equatable, Sendable {
    let latitude: Double
    let longitude: Double
}

enum PositioningError: Error, Equatable {
    case denied
}

protocol PositioningDelegate: AnyObject, Sendable {
    func positioning(didUpdate fix: Fix)
    func positioning(didFail error: PositioningError)
}

/// A delegate-based API that holds its delegate weakly, as most do.
final class LegacyPositioning: Sendable {
    private let delegateBox = Mutex<(any PositioningDelegate)?>(nil)
    private let running = Mutex(false)

    func setDelegate(_ delegate: any PositioningDelegate) {
        delegateBox.withLock { $0 = delegate }
    }

    func startUpdates(fixes: [Fix], thenFail error: PositioningError? = nil) {
        running.withLock { $0 = true }
        DispatchQueue.global().async { [self] in
            for fix in fixes {
                guard running.withLock({ $0 }) else { return }
                delegateBox.withLock { $0 }?.positioning(didUpdate: fix)
                usleep(2_000)
            }
            if let error {
                delegateBox.withLock { $0 }?.positioning(didFail: error)
            }
        }
    }

    func stopUpdates() {
        running.withLock { $0 = false }
        delegateBox.withLock { $0 = nil }
    }

    var isRunning: Bool {
        running.withLock { $0 }
    }
}

/// Forwards delegate calls into a throwing stream's continuation.
final class PositioningStreamAdapter: PositioningDelegate {
    let continuation: AsyncThrowingStream<Fix, any Error>.Continuation

    init(continuation: AsyncThrowingStream<Fix, any Error>.Continuation) {
        self.continuation = continuation
    }

    func positioning(didUpdate fix: Fix) {
        continuation.yield(fix)
    }

    func positioning(didFail error: PositioningError) {
        continuation.finish(throwing: error)
    }
}

extension LegacyPositioning {
    func fixes(_ simulated: [Fix], thenFail error: PositioningError? = nil) -> AsyncThrowingStream<Fix, any Error> {
        let (stream, continuation) = AsyncThrowingStream.makeStream(of: Fix.self, throwing: (any Error).self)
        let adapter = PositioningStreamAdapter(continuation: continuation)
        setDelegate(adapter)
        continuation.onTermination = { [self] _ in
            _ = adapter          // Keeps the delegate alive exactly as long as the stream.
            stopUpdates()
        }
        startUpdates(fixes: simulated, thenFail: error)
        return stream
    }
}

let positioning = LegacyPositioning()
let route = [Fix(latitude: 1, longitude: 1), Fix(latitude: 2, longitude: 2)]
var tracked: [Fix] = []
do {
    for try await fix in positioning.fixes(route, thenFail: .denied) {
        tracked.append(fix)
    }
    assertionFailure("The stream must end with the delegate's error")
} catch PositioningError.denied {
}
assert(tracked == route)
assert(!positioning.isRunning, "Finishing with an error ran onTermination, which stopped updates")

AsyncThrowingStream adds finish(throwing:), which ends the stream with an error: the consumer receives every buffered element first, then the error from for try await. The delegate’s failure callback maps onto it directly.

The ownership arrangement is worth copying. The legacy API holds its delegate weakly, so something else must keep the adapter alive. Capturing it in onTermination ties its lifetime to the stream’s: alive while anyone might read, released when the stream terminates. The _ = adapter line exists only to make the capture explicit.

The lifecycle rules, tested

A stream terminates exactly once, for one of two reasons, which onTermination receives:

  • .finished: the producer called finish() or finish(throwing:).
  • .cancelled: the consumer’s task was cancelled, or the last reference to the stream and its iterator was released. A cancellation is noticed when the consumer is waiting in next() or next calls it; the backpressure article shows what that means for buffered values.

After termination, yield returns .terminated and drops the value. Producers should treat that as a signal to stop:

let terminationReasons = Mutex<[String]>([])

let (finishedStream, finishedContinuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
finishedContinuation.onTermination = { reason in
    terminationReasons.withLock { $0.append("\(reason)") }
}
finishedContinuation.yield(7)
finishedContinuation.finish()
if case .terminated = finishedContinuation.yield(8) {} else {
    assertionFailure("Yielding after finish reports termination")
}
var afterFinish: [Int] = []
for await value in finishedStream {
    afterFinish.append(value)
}
assert(afterFinish == [7], "Values buffered before finish() are still delivered")

let (cancelledStream, cancelledContinuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
cancelledContinuation.onTermination = { reason in
    terminationReasons.withLock { $0.append("\(reason)") }
}
let cancelledConsumer = Task {
    for await _ in cancelledStream {}
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(10))
cancelledConsumer.cancel()
await cancelledConsumer.value
if case .terminated = cancelledContinuation.yield(1) {} else {
    assertionFailure("Yielding after the consumer left reports termination")
}
assert(terminationReasons.withLock { $0 } == ["finished", "cancelled"])

Two rules are easy to get wrong because they differ from what many people expect.

Breaking out of a loop does not, by itself, terminate the stream. A stream terminates with .cancelled when the consuming task is cancelled, or when the last copy of the stream and its iterators is released. If the stream is still referenced, by a stored property, a variable in an enclosing scope, or top-level code, then leaving the loop leaves the stream alive and its producer running:

let stillRunning = LegacyTicker()
let storedTicks = stillRunning.ticks(every: .milliseconds(5))   // Kept in a variable.

func readTwo(from stream: AsyncStream<Int>) async -> [Int] {
    var values: [Int] = []
    for await value in stream {
        values.append(value)
        if values.count == 2 { break }
    }
    return values
}

let twoTicks = await readTwo(from: storedTicks)
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))
assert(twoTicks == [1, 2])
assert(stillRunning.isRunning, "The stream is still referenced, so it never terminated")
stillRunning.stop()

On the test toolchain, a stream created inside a function terminated as soon as the function returned, while the same loop over a stored stream, or over a stream in top-level code, left the producer running indefinitely. If a stream must be stored, cancel the task that consumes it, or finish it from the producer side, rather than relying on break.

Releasing the continuation does not finish the stream. If a producer object holding the only continuation is deallocated without calling finish(), the consumer waits forever:

func streamWhoseProducerForgetsToFinish() -> AsyncStream<Int> {
    let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Int.self)
    continuation.yield(1)
    return stream        // The continuation is released here; finish() is never called.
}

let forgotten = streamWhoseProducerForgetsToFinish()
let stuckConsumer = Task { () -> [Int] in
    var values: [Int] = []
    for await value in forgotten {
        values.append(value)
    }
    return values
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(100))
// Still waiting after 100 ms; only cancellation ends the loop.
stuckConsumer.cancel()
let stuckValues = await stuckConsumer.value
assert(stuckValues == [1])

On the test toolchain, the consumer stayed suspended for as long as it was left, and only cancelling it ended the loop. Make finishing part of the producer’s teardown: call finish() from the producer’s deinit or stop() method, and from every error path.

One stream, one consumer

AsyncStream delivers each element once. If two tasks iterate the same stream, they compete for elements: each element goes to whichever consumer is waiting, and neither sees the whole sequence. On the test toolchain this did not crash, but it is almost never what the code intended.

When several consumers need every event, give each its own stream. A broadcaster keeps one continuation per subscriber, removes it when that subscriber’s stream terminates, and yields each event to all of them:

/// Fans each event out to every current subscriber. Each subscriber gets its own stream.
final class Broadcaster<Event: Sendable>: Sendable {
    private let subscribers = Mutex<Set<AsyncStream<Event>.Continuation>>([])

    func subscribe(bufferingNewest limit: Int = 16) -> AsyncStream<Event> {
        let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Event.self, bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(limit))
        subscribers.withLock { _ = $0.insert(continuation) }
        continuation.onTermination = { [weak self] _ in
            self?.subscribers.withLock { _ = $0.remove(continuation) }
        }
        return stream
    }

    func send(_ event: Event) {
        for subscriber in subscribers.withLock({ $0 }) {
            subscriber.yield(event)
        }
    }

    func finish() {
        let all = subscribers.withLock { all in
            defer { all.removeAll() }
            return all
        }
        for subscriber in all {
            subscriber.finish()
        }
    }

    var subscriberCount: Int {
        subscribers.withLock { $0.count }
    }
}

let events = Broadcaster<String>()
let firstReader = Task { () -> [String] in
    var seen: [String] = []
    for await event in events.subscribe() { seen.append(event) }
    return seen
}
let secondReader = Task { () -> [String] in
    var seen: [String] = []
    for await event in events.subscribe() {
        seen.append(event)
        if seen.count == 1 { break }      // This subscriber leaves early; its stream is released with the task.
    }
    return seen
}
while events.subscriberCount < 2 {
    await Task.yield()
}
events.send("login")
_ = await secondReader.value
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(10))
assert(events.subscriberCount == 1, "The departed subscriber removed itself")
events.send("purchase")
events.finish()
let firstSeen = await firstReader.value
let secondSeen = await secondReader.value
assert(firstSeen == ["login", "purchase"])
assert(secondSeen == ["login"])

Storing continuations in a Set relies on AsyncStream.Continuation being Hashable, added in Swift 6.2 (SE-0468); before that, the usual approach was a dictionary keyed by a UUID. Copying the set out of the lock before yielding keeps yield calls, which can resume consumers, outside the critical section.

Each subscriber’s buffer is bounded at 16 newest events, so a slow subscriber drops old events instead of growing without limit. Choosing that policy deliberately is the subject of the next article.

Pull-based streams with unfolding

AsyncStream(unfolding:onCancel:) builds a stream from a closure that produces the next element on demand. Unlike the continuation-based form, it is pull-based: the closure runs only when the consumer asks for an element, so there is no buffer to manage.

let idCounter = Mutex(0)
let identifiers = AsyncStream<Int>(unfolding: {
    let next = idCounter.withLock { counter -> Int in
        counter += 1
        return counter
    }
    return next <= 5 ? next : nil
})

var collectedIDs: [Int] = []
for await id in identifiers {
    collectedIDs.append(id)
}
assert(collectedIDs == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
assert(idCounter.withLock { $0 } == 6, "The closure ran once per element, plus once to end")

Use unfolding when the source can produce on request, such as reading from a queue or generating values. Use the continuation-based form when the source pushes on its own schedule, as callbacks and delegates do.

Summary

  • AsyncStream.makeStream returns a Sendable continuation for the producer and a stream for one consumer. yield never suspends.
  • Adapt callback and delegate APIs by yielding from the callback and stopping the producer in onTermination, which runs on both finishing and cancellation.
  • AsyncThrowingStream.finish(throwing:) maps failure callbacks onto stream errors, after buffered elements are delivered.
  • After termination, yield returns .terminated; producers should stop.
  • A stream terminates when its consumer’s task is cancelled or its last reference is released, not when a loop breaks. Do not rely on break to stop a stored stream.
  • Releasing the continuation does not finish the stream. Always call finish() on every producer exit path.
  • A stream has one consumer; concurrent iterators split its elements. Broadcast by giving each subscriber its own stream.
  • AsyncStream(unfolding:) is pull-based and needs no buffer.

Exercise

Wrap URLSession’s delegate-based download progress into an AsyncThrowingStream<Progress, any Error> that yields fractional progress values and finishes with the downloaded file’s URL as a final event, or with an error. Retain the delegate through onTermination, cancel the download task when the consumer stops iterating, and test three cases with URLProtocol fixtures: normal completion, a server error, and a consumer that breaks out of the loop at 50%.

Further reading

  • SE-0314: AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream.
  • SE-0388: Convenience Async[Throwing]Stream.makeStream methods.
  • SE-0468: Hashable conformance for Async(Throwing)Stream.Continuation.
  • Meet AsyncSequence, WWDC21.

entry.summary: Most event sources in an app were built before Swift concurrency: delegates that report location fixes, callbacks that fire for every download chunk, observers that receive notifications, timers that tick. AsyncStream and AsyncThrowingStream adapt them to AsyncSequence, so consumers can write for await event in events and get cancellation, structured lifetimes, and sequential processing for free. The adapter has two halves: a continuation that the producer pushes values into, and a stream that one consumer iterates. Getting the boundary right means deciding who finishes the stream, what happens when the consumer goes away, and what to do when there is more than one consumer. This article builds adapters for a callback API and a delegate API, shows the lifecycle rules with tests, and fixes the single-consumer limitation with a broadcaster.

entry.title: Consuming Values with AsyncSequence in Swift

link.title: Consuming Values with AsyncSequence in Swift

entry.content:
An async function produces one value, later. An AsyncSequence produces many values over time: lines of a file as they are read, pages of an API as they are fetched, notifications as they are posted, model changes as they happen. Consuming one looks like an ordinary loop, for await value in sequence, and the familiar operators map, filter, prefix, and reduce all work.

The similarity to Sequence is deliberate, and it hides the properties that matter in practice: iteration is pull-based and lazy, each element costs an await, a sequence may or may not restart when iterated twice, and what happens on cancellation is up to each sequence. This article covers consuming the built-in sequences, writing your own with typed errors, and the performance and lifetime rules that keep stream-processing code correct.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain on macOS 26. Performance numbers quoted in the text come from an optimized build on an Apple M1 Ultra. The Swift blocks build on one another in one main.swift.

The protocol

protocol AsyncSequence<Element, Failure> {
    associatedtype AsyncIterator: AsyncIteratorProtocol
    associatedtype Element
    associatedtype Failure: Error = any Error
    func makeAsyncIterator() -> AsyncIterator
}

protocol AsyncIteratorProtocol<Element, Failure> {
    mutating func next() async throws(Failure) -> Element?
}

That is a simplified view of the declarations, which also include an isolation-aware next(isolation:) requirement. Since Swift 6.0, both protocols have a Failure associated type (SE-0421), so a sequence can declare that it never throws, throws any Error, or throws one specific error type. Primary associated types allow some AsyncSequence<Int, Never> in signatures.

for await element in sequence is sugar for creating an iterator and calling next() until it returns nil. The loop body runs in the consumer’s task and isolation; next() is an ordinary async call that may suspend.

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: The consumer pulls each element by awaiting next on the iterator
    participant C as Consumer loop
    participant I as Iterator
    participant S as Source, for example a file or an API
    C->>I: await next()
    I->>S: read or fetch as needed
    S-->>I: data
    I-->>C: element 1
    Note over C: Loop body runs, iterator is idle
    C->>I: await next()
    I-->>C: element 2
    C->>I: await next()
    I-->>C: nil, sequence finished

Nothing happens between calls. The iterator produces an element only when the consumer asks for one, so a slow consumer automatically slows the producer. That is pull-based iteration, and it is the most important difference from push-based streams like AsyncStream, which the next article covers.

Consuming built-in sequences

Foundation provides asynchronous sequences for common sources. Reading a file line by line, for example, uses URL.lines:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

let logURL = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory
    .appendingPathComponent("asyncsequence-\(UUID().uuidString).log")
let logLines = (1...1_000).map { index in
    index % 10 == 0 ? "ERROR request \(index) failed" : "INFO request \(index) ok"
}
try logLines.joined(separator: "\n").write(to: logURL, atomically: true, encoding: .utf8)

var errorCount = 0
for try await line in logURL.lines where line.hasPrefix("ERROR") {
    errorCount += 1
}
assert(errorCount == 100)

The same operators as on Sequence exist, each returning a new lazy asynchronous sequence or awaiting a result:

let firstErrors = try await logURL.lines
    .filter { $0.hasPrefix("ERROR") }
    .map { $0.split(separator: " ")[2] }
    .prefix(3)
    .reduce(into: [String]()) { $0.append(String($1)) }
assert(firstErrors == ["10", "20", "30"])

let containsRequest500 = try await logURL.lines.contains { $0.contains("request 500 ") }
assert(containsRequest500)
try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: logURL)

Because the chain is lazy and pull-based, prefix(3) stops the whole pipeline after the third matching line: the file is not read to the end. contains stops at the first match.

Other built-in sources include URL.resourceBytes and FileHandle.bytes for raw bytes, URLSession.bytes(for:) for streaming HTTP responses, NotificationCenter.notifications(named:) for notifications, and, from Swift 6.2, Observations for changes to @Observable state, shown in the main actor article.

Each element costs an await

Every next() is an async call. Even when it does not suspend, it has overhead: an iterator call, sometimes a buffer refill, sometimes an executor check. For a sequence of many tiny elements, that overhead dominates. If each element costs \(c\) in iteration overhead and \(t\) in useful work, throughput is bounded by

\[\text{elements per second} \le \frac{1}{c + t}.\]

On the test machine, reading a 2.7 MB file containing 200,000 short lines took, in an optimized build:

Approach Elements Time Per element
for try await over url.lines 200,000 lines 1.19 s about 6 µs
for try await over url.resourceBytes 2.7 million bytes 0.17 s about 63 ns
Data(contentsOf:), all at once 1 buffer 0.0007 s not applicable

The lesson is not that async sequences are slow; it is that element granularity matters. Byte-at-a-time iteration of a large local file costs about 230 times more than reading it in one call. For local files that fit in memory, read them whole and process the buffer synchronously, ideally off the main actor. Use byte and line sequences for sources that genuinely arrive over time, such as network streams and pipes, where waiting dominates and incremental processing lets you start before the end arrives.

Writing an AsyncSequence: a paginated API

A paginated API is a natural asynchronous sequence: each page is fetched only when the consumer is ready for it. Declaring a concrete Failure type lets the compiler know exactly what the loop can throw:

enum FeedError: Error, Equatable {
    case offline
    case badPage(Int)
}

/// A fake backend that counts its fetches so laziness can be observed.
final class FeedBackend: Sendable {
    private let fetches = Mutex(0)
    let pageCount: Int
    let failingPage: Int?

    init(pageCount: Int, failingPage: Int? = nil) {
        self.pageCount = pageCount
        self.failingPage = failingPage
    }

    func fetchPage(_ page: Int) async throws(FeedError) -> [String]? {
        fetches.withLock { $0 += 1 }
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(2))
        if page == failingPage { throw .badPage(page) }
        guard page < pageCount else { return nil }
        return (0..<3).map { "post \(page * 3 + $0)" }
    }

    var fetchCount: Int {
        fetches.withLock { $0 }
    }
}

struct FeedPages: AsyncSequence {
    typealias Element = [String]
    typealias Failure = FeedError

    let backend: FeedBackend

    struct AsyncIterator: AsyncIteratorProtocol {
        let backend: FeedBackend
        var nextPage = 0
        var finished = false

        mutating func next() async throws(FeedError) -> [String]? {
            guard !finished, !Task.isCancelled else { return nil }
            guard let page = try await backend.fetchPage(nextPage) else {
                finished = true
                return nil
            }
            nextPage += 1
            return page
        }
    }

    func makeAsyncIterator() -> AsyncIterator {
        AsyncIterator(backend: backend)
    }
}

Consumers iterate it like any other sequence. The catch clause receives a FeedError, not any Error, because the sequence’s Failure is concrete:

let backend = FeedBackend(pageCount: 4)
var posts: [String] = []
for try await page in FeedPages(backend: backend) {
    posts += page
}
assert(posts.count == 12)
assert(backend.fetchCount == 5, "Four pages plus the fetch that discovered the end")

let brokenBackend = FeedBackend(pageCount: 4, failingPage: 2)
do {
    for try await _ in FeedPages(backend: brokenBackend) {}
    assertionFailure("Page 2 must fail")
} catch {
    let typed: FeedError = error       // The error is statically a FeedError.
    assert(typed == .badPage(2))
}

Laziness is observable through the fetch count. A consumer that needs only the first few posts fetches only the pages that contain them:

let lazyBackend = FeedBackend(pageCount: 100)
let firstFivePosts = try await FeedPages(backend: lazyBackend)
    .flatMap { $0.async }
    .prefix(5)
    .reduce(into: [String]()) { $0.append($1) }
assert(firstFivePosts == ["post 0", "post 1", "post 2", "post 3", "post 4"])
assert(lazyBackend.fetchCount == 2, "Only two of a hundred pages were fetched")

The .async property on an array, defined below, turns a synchronous collection into an asynchronous sequence so that flatMap can splice pages into a stream of posts. It is the one piece of glue the standard library does not provide:

struct AsyncCollection<Base: Collection & Sendable>: AsyncSequence, Sendable where Base.Element: Sendable {
    typealias Element = Base.Element
    typealias Failure = Never

    let base: Base

    struct AsyncIterator: AsyncIteratorProtocol {
        var iterator: Base.Iterator

        mutating func next() async -> Base.Element? {
            iterator.next()
        }
    }

    func makeAsyncIterator() -> AsyncIterator {
        AsyncIterator(iterator: base.makeIterator())
    }
}

extension Collection where Self: Sendable, Element: Sendable {
    var async: AsyncCollection<Self> {
        AsyncCollection(base: self)
    }
}

The swift-async-algorithms package provides this and many more operators, such as merge, zip, debounce, throttle, and chunked, if you need them across a codebase.

Iterating twice

Sequence makes no promise that iterating twice yields the same elements, and neither does AsyncSequence. In practice, sequences fall into two groups:

  • Restartable sequences create independent state in makeAsyncIterator(). FeedPages is one: each loop starts at page zero and fetches everything again. So is url.lines, which reopens the file.
  • Single-consumer streams share one underlying source. AsyncStream and NotificationCenter.notifications(named:) deliver each element once; two loops compete for elements rather than both receiving them.
let restartBackend = FeedBackend(pageCount: 2)
let feed = FeedPages(backend: restartBackend)
var firstPass = 0
for try await page in feed { firstPass += page.count }
var secondPass = 0
for try await page in feed { secondPass += page.count }
assert(firstPass == 6 && secondPass == 6)
assert(restartBackend.fetchCount == 6, "The second loop fetched every page again")

Document which kind your sequence is. For an API-backed sequence, a second iteration that silently re-fetches everything is a performance bug waiting to happen; caching or a single shared stream may be what callers actually want.

Cancellation ends iteration, in the sequence’s own way

When the task running a for await loop is cancelled, the loop does not stop by itself. It stops when next() returns nil or throws. Each sequence decides which:

  • AsyncStream delivers anything already buffered, then returns nil, so the loop ends normally; the backpressure article traces the exact order.
  • FeedPages above checks Task.isCancelled and returns nil.
  • URLSession.bytes(for:) throws URLError(.cancelled).
  • A sequence that never checks keeps producing elements until it is exhausted.
let endlessBackend = FeedBackend(pageCount: 1_000)
let reader = Task { () -> Int in
    var pages = 0
    for try await _ in FeedPages(backend: endlessBackend) {
        pages += 1
    }
    return pages
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(30))
reader.cancel()
let pagesBeforeCancellation = try await reader.value
assert(pagesBeforeCancellation < 1_000, "The iterator noticed cancellation and finished early")

Returning nil on cancellation makes cancelled iteration look like a normal end of sequence, which is convenient in loops but can hide the cancellation from code after the loop. Throwing CancellationError makes it explicit. Either is defensible; choose one, and check Task.isCancelled after the loop if the distinction matters.

Long-lived loops need owners

A loop over an infinite sequence, such as notifications, location updates, or model observations, never ends on its own. The task running it must be owned and cancelled, exactly like the polling loops in the task lifetime article:

@MainActor
final class ThemeObserver {
    private(set) var changes = 0
    private var observation: Task<Void, Never>?

    func start() {
        observation = Task { [weak self] in
            for await _ in NotificationCenter.default.notifications(named: .themeDidChange) {
                guard let self else { return }
                self.changes += 1
            }
        }
    }

    func stop() {
        observation?.cancel()
        observation = nil
    }
}

extension Notification.Name {
    static let themeDidChange = Notification.Name("ThemeDidChange")
}

let themeObserver = ThemeObserver()
themeObserver.start()
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))
NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .themeDidChange, object: nil)
NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .themeDidChange, object: nil)
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))
assert(themeObserver.changes == 2)
themeObserver.stop()
NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .themeDidChange, object: nil)
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(20))
assert(themeObserver.changes == 2, "No more changes after stop()")

The guard let self inside the loop, rather than before it, lets the observer deallocate even if nobody calls stop(): each element re-checks the weak reference. Calling stop() explicitly is still better, because the loop otherwise lingers until the next notification arrives.

Processing elements concurrently

A for await loop processes elements one at a time: the next element is not requested until the body finishes. That is often correct, because order is preserved and back-pressure is automatic, but it serializes work that could overlap. To process elements concurrently with a limit, combine the loop with a task group’s sliding window, from the task groups article:

func processConcurrently(pages: FeedPages, maxInFlight: Int) async throws -> Int {
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Int.self) { group in
        var inFlight = 0
        var processed = 0
        for try await page in pages {
            if inFlight == maxInFlight {
                processed += try await group.next() ?? 0
                inFlight -= 1
            }
            group.addTask {
                try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(5))      // Per-page work.
                return page.count
            }
            inFlight += 1
        }
        for try await count in group {
            processed += count
        }
        return processed
    }
}

let concurrentBackend = FeedBackend(pageCount: 10)
let processedPosts = try await processConcurrently(pages: FeedPages(backend: concurrentBackend), maxInFlight: 3)
assert(processedPosts == 30)

The consumer still pulls pages one at a time, but it no longer waits for each page’s processing before pulling the next, up to three at once. Results arrive in completion order; attach indices, as the task groups article shows, if order matters.

Summary

  • AsyncSequence is a pull-based, lazy sequence whose next() is async. Since Swift 6.0 it has a Failure type, so sequences can declare precise errors.
  • The standard operators work and stay lazy: prefix, first, and contains stop the pipeline early.
  • Each element costs an await. Measured overhead was about 63 ns per byte and 6 µs per line; choose element granularity accordingly.
  • Write custom sequences as an iterator with a mutating next(); check cancellation and decide whether it returns nil or throws.
  • Know whether a sequence restarts on each iteration or is a single shared stream, and document it.
  • Infinite loops need an owning task with a stop(); concurrent processing needs a bounded task group around the loop.

Exercise

Write struct LogTail: AsyncSequence that yields new lines appended to a file, polling the file size every 50 ms and reading only the new bytes. Give it a concrete Failure type, return nil when the task is cancelled, and make it restartable from the current end of the file. Test it by appending lines from another task while a consumer reads with prefix(10), and verify that the poller stops once prefix is satisfied.

Further reading

  • SE-0298: Async/Await: Sequences.
  • SE-0421: Generalize effect polymorphism for AsyncSequence and AsyncIteratorProtocol.
  • swift-async-algorithms for merge, zip, debounce, chunked, and more.
  • Meet AsyncSequence, WWDC21.

entry.summary: An async function produces one value, later. An AsyncSequence produces many values over time: lines of a file as they are read, pages of an API as they are fetched, notifications as they are posted, model changes as they happen. Consuming one looks like an ordinary loop, for await value in sequence, and the familiar operators map, filter, prefix, and reduce all work. The similarity to Sequence is deliberate, and it hides the properties that matter in practice: iteration is pull-based and lazy, each element costs an await, a sequence may or may not restart when iterated twice, and what happens on cancellation is up to each sequence. This article covers consuming the built-in sequences, writing your own with typed errors, and the performance and lifetime rules that keep stream-processing code correct.
